title: WorkSafe investigates shovel fire at Kalgoorlie Super Pit
text:
WorkSafe WA is investigating after a fire engulfed the driver's cab of a heavy-duty mining shovel at one of Australia's biggest gold mines.

The incident occurred last Wednesday during the night shift while the 750-tonne Komatsu PC8000 shovel was working in the Oroya Brownhill section of Kalgoorlie's Super Pit, about 600 kilometres east of Perth.

The Super Pit's owner, gold miner Northern Star Resources, confirmed no one was injured in the incident.

The cause of the fire has not been disclosed at this stage.

A Komatsu PC8000 shovel operating at Kalgoorlie's Super Pit gold mine. (Supplied: Northern Star Resources/Dianne Newell)

'No disruption' to mine

In a statement to the ABC, Northern Star said the mine operator Kalgoorlie Consolidated Gold Mines (KCGM) immediately activated its emergency response team, which extinguished the fire.

A Northern Star spokesperson said there has been no material interruption to Super Pit operations.

"KCGM has initiated contingency plans to cover for the damaged excavator, which in any event was due to be retired in November 2026 and replaced by a new excavator," they said.

"In line with our normal processes, the KCGM team is carrying out a thorough assessment of the incident so that we can apply learnings, strengthen our processes and continue safe and reliable operations."

WorkSafe WA said it was aware of the incident and was investigating the circumstances surrounding the fire.

The Super Pit gold mine has been operating since 1989. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

According to Northern Star, the PC8000 is one of the biggest mechanical shovels in the world and has an estimated replacement cost of $18 million.

Its fuel tank has a capacity of 13,900 litres of diesel, and one full bucket of material is equal to 68.5 tonnes.

The damaged machine is one of four PC8000 shovels in the open pit fleet at the Super Pit, which also includes 45 Caterpillar 793F trucks with a 226-tonne payload and five newer 793NG trucks.

New shovel on the way

The fire comes just weeks after Northern Star put a retired PC8000 shovel on display at the Super Pit's public lookout, which attracts thousands of locals and tourists every year.

The company has ruled out returning that shovel to service.

Mining equipment supplier Liebherr delivered a new 600-tonne R9600 excavator to the Super Pit in July, with a second shovel due to arrive in October.

A decommissioned PC8000 shovel was put on display at the Super Pit public lookout in August. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

The Super Pit employs more than 1,200 workers, and has had about 600 contractors on site during the past three years to complete a $1.7 billion expansion of the Fimiston Mill, which is now being commissioned.

After a two-year ramp-up of the new mill, the Super Pit is forecast to grow production from 480,429 ounces in the 2025-26 financial year to 900,000 ounces a year from 2028-29.

If it hits that mark, it would reclaim the title of Australia's biggest producing gold mine from Boddington in WA's South West.

title: The National's Bryce Dessner on the concert hall vs the algorithm
text:
Bryce Dessner has always lived across two worlds.

He is the guitarist and keyboardist in The National, one of indie rock's most successful and prestigious acts, which he co-founded in 1999.

At the same time, he was a classically trained Yale graduate who composed and performed experimental music around Brooklyn into the early 2000s.

He has won Grammys for both alternative and chamber music albums, earned a Best Original Song Oscar for Train Dreams, co-written with Nick Cave, collaborated with minimalist masters Philip Glass and Steve Reich, and penned orchestrations for Paul Simon, Bon Iver and Taylor Swift (on albums produced by his twin and The National bandmate Aaron Dessner).

This month, he teams with the Sydney Symphony Orchestra for the first solo Australian tour of his orchestral work.

Bryce Dessner with his band mates in indie rock darlings, The National (Supplied: Graham MacIndoe)

Dessner views both disciplines as complementary.

"They're actually kind of similar," he tells Double J. "They're this collaborative, very human archetype of people who work together week in, week out on music."

The big difference? The National composes together whereas, with an orchestra, "I have to show up with a fully completed score. It doesn't mean the collaboration is any less deep or important; it's just a different process".

Then there is the grander scale an orchestra provides: "I can really dig in deeper, and there's lots of colours to explore."

He compares it to writing poetry versus an epic novel. This month he'll showcase his newest musical chapter: the Australian debut of his cello concerto Trembling Earth

The political and the pastoral

Trembling Earth was inspired by an Oslo exhibition of landscape paintings by Edvard Munch.

"They were pre-World War I, probably a similar time [to now] in terms of the intensity of situations playing out on a global scale," says Dessner, who grew up in Ohio surrounded by maple and cedar trees.

"I found it so moving.

"He's painting these old oak woods … so full of emotion and tragedy."

It recalls a quote from German painter Anselm Kiefer: "There is no such thing as an innocent landscape."

"Trembling Earth is like a pastoral symphony but reflecting on the state of the human condition," Dessner says.

" I didn't necessarily want to make a really political piece, but obviously the times we're living in are so difficult, traumatic and full of conflict. "

As the Czech Philharmonic's inaugural composer-in-residence, Dessner wrote Trembling Earth for Russian cello virtuoso Anastasia Kobekina.

He calls Kobekina a "force of nature" who can play all the classics ("Dvorak, Elgar, Tchaikovsky") but also loves new music "like Radiohead and Aphex Twin".

Loading Instagram content

Kobekina is the concerto's axis, animating its melodic, lyrical moments and bringing a forceful intensity that evokes the rhythmic power of Shostakovich or Stravinsky.

"She's one of the premier soloists in the world, so it's a big deal for Australian audiences to hear her," Dessner says.

Landscape is a unifying force in Dessner's music.

Impermanence, an award-winning work commissioned by the Australian String Quartet and Sydney Dance Company, was written in response to Australia's devastating Black Summer bushfires.

Set to Rafael Bonachela's visceral choreography, it juxtaposes beauty and devastation. Those themes extend to Trembling Earth, where calamity and renewal co-exist.

"The way the Earth bears witness to the effects of humanity's bad decision-making," explains Dessner. "And that, despite its fragility, spring does come. There's a sense of renewal and hope in these pieces."

St Carolyn By The Sea, another Australian premiere, features two electric guitars that function like harps, overlapping in waves against strings ranging from soft to frenzied.

Loading Instagram content

It was inspired by Jack Kerouac's 1962 novel Big Sur, written while the author battled alcoholism and declining mental health.

"He wrote it about the west coast and the Pacific Ocean," Dessner says. "But also mentioning Stravinsky, John Coltrane and Beethoven. It just felt vast and orchestral.

"This endless sky, the sense of the ocean – the orchestral sound can really do that."

The concert hall vs the algorithm

The orchestra's size and scope allow Dessner to translate landscape into sound. But both his classical and rock backgrounds serve similar artistic impulses: capturing emotion and the fragility of the human condition.

In the age of what he calls "algorithmic culture", feeds bombarded by "AI and computer-driven music, where we don't even know if it's a human being behind it", Dessner argues live music and human connection matter more, not less.

"The concert hall itself has become this kind of haven, this human temple of creativity," he says.

"Let's get off our phones and listen to live music, not be filming it. Just be in the space with sound, with musicians who spent their lives playing these instruments.

"It's an interesting time. People are freaking out about seeing AI artists on Spotify. I don't think we're going to see that in the concert hall; robots on stage playing Beethoven or something.

Bryce Dessner now lives in southern France with wife Pauline (aka artist Mia Tindle) and children. (Supplied: Anne Mie Dreves)

Dessner remains busy. He recently finished his first opera, Herakles Mad, "which I'm really happy about," that opens next year.

Next month, The National reunite for a one-off show; their first since a "good, healthy break" from intense touring supporting back-to-back 2023 albums First Two Pages of Frankenstein and Laugh Track.

The National & Fleet Foxes are a perfect double bill. But too much of a good thing? A back-to-back evening of prestige indie rock, with Fleet Foxes' majestic folk complementing The National's artfully maudlin poetry.

It is not too soon to talk about a follow-up.

"We never turn it off. Matt [Berninger, vocalist] sent me something last week," Dessner reveals.

"We don't have a deadline or a plan necessarily, but we're starting to veer back towards each other."

It is a wonder Dessner finds time to sustain his many creative threads.

"There's seasons of things … moving calendars," he says.

"It can get lonely. And writing a concerto can feel like climbing Mount Everest.

"I told myself, 'You know what? I do this because I love it'. I try to keep track of that … that I'm enjoying doing it. That keeps me grounded."

Turning 50 prompted reflection on his achievements – and his shrinking bucket list.

"There was a time when I was like, 'Oh god, I really want to write a string quartet or orchestral piece'. I've done quite a few of these things now, and I'm proud of the music," he says.

"It really becomes a choice of, 'What am I most excited to do?' And keeping track of what I have to say, and enjoying that time."

Bryce Dessner's Trembling Earth, with Anastasia Kobekina and Umberto Cleriici, is at the Sydney Opera House on September 19 and 20.

Bryce Dessner and The Sydney Symphony's A Portrait In Music, September 24 at Sydney City Recital Hall and September 25 at Melbourne Recital Centre.

title: I'm ready to be Swans captain, says Gulden
text:
Sydney superstar Errol Gulden says he is prepared to step up as captain to help the Swans pursue an AFL premiership bid without the injured Callum Mills.

The 24-year-old has thrown his hat in the ring to deputise for skipper Mills after his midfield performance led the Swans to a stirring qualifying final win over Brisbane.

Sydney coach Dean Cox also has an experienced leader in former co-captain Dane Rampe, as well as fellow veteran Jake Lloyd, midfielder James Rowbottom and Tom Papley at his disposal.

Whoever Cox lands on could also play a key leadership role next year, with Mills facing the possibility of missing the entire 2027 season after tearing the anterior cruciate ligament in his right knee.

Swans vice-captain Isaac Heeney is among five players serving club-imposed bans after last month's post-match incident at the Pullman Hotel in Melbourne.

Star defender Mills had earned significant praise for leading the Swans through the turmoil, which past players said shattered the club's famed "Bloods culture".

Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, James Jordon and Riley Bice are the other Swans who will not play again this season.

Gulden rallied the Swans after Mills went down late in the first quarter against the back-to-back reigning premiers, finishing with one goal, 34 disposals and eight clearances.

"If it [the captaincy] was offered to me, I would love to," Gulden told AAP.

"I would feel like I'd be ready. I wouldn't change anything that I'm doing. I don't think any of us need to change anything that we're doing.

"But you're just so shattered for the person. He's [Mills] just an amazing leader.

"He is the best human being at the club. It's just not fair.

"We've just got to keep going, and it's going to be next man in."

Gulden said the 53-point qualifying final win left him with the most pride he has ever felt in the Swans across six seasons at the club.

The two-time All-Australian has played in two losing grand finals (2022, 2024), with last year's 10th-placed finish the first time he had missed finals in his career.

"I love playing with this team. The last couple of games have been so fun as a player to be a part of," Gulden said.

"There's something in having your back against the wall and trying to fight your way out of it.

"The weekend [against the Lions] was easily the most rewarding game.

"The most pride I've felt to be a part of this team in my career.

"There was obviously some respect lost for the club. It's completely fair enough.

Scans confirm ACL rupture for Swans skipper Callum Mills will be sidelined for the remainder of Sydney's finals campaign and possibly all of next season after scans revealed an ACL tear in his right knee.

"All we can focus on as players is what we can control, and that's going out there and representing the club the best way we can on and off the field.

"I'm really proud of the club and the team, everyone involved, because the last few weeks have been really difficult."

Sydney will continue its unlikely flag push by hosting minor premiers Fremantle at the SCG on Friday.

"A premiership would mean the absolute world to me," Gulden said.

"Even if what happened hadn't happened, it still would mean the world to me."

AAP

title: 'You've got to be loyal, good times and bad': Crows fans commiserate finals loss
text:
Crows fans were flying high before their grand final dreams were smashed by the Brisbane Lions at the Gabba with a 53-point feat on Saturday night.

Fans who could not make it to the game in Brisbane gathered at venues around Adelaide to watch the match.

At half-time the Crows trailed by 38 points but some fans remained optimistic.

"It's going to be a grind to get back in it, we were nearly there, weren't we," Lee Mason said during the break in play.

Others though were not so sure.

"Good for about five minutes in the second quarter, and we were all up and about, getting a bit rowdy with it, but since then it's been nothing really," Blake Kerley said.

Mr Kerley said watching a not-so-distant 2017 grand final made him want to stick with his team.

"That heartbreak, and you ride with them through the highs and lows," Mr Kerley said.

Longtime fan Jenni Read-Smith had a similar view.

"You've got to be loyal, good times and bad times, you can't be a fair-weather supporter … that's what team sport is all about," Ms Read-Smith said.

George Koutsamanis says the team "fought well" but finals are "never easy". (ABC News: Will Hunter)

George Koutsamanis told the ABC at half-time that it would be a difficult road to victory.

"You let a team kick five goals in five minutes — it's a long way back," he said.

"The team's done well, they've fought well, but the finals are never easy, to be the best, you've got to beat the best."

When it was all over for the Crows, Jimmy Pritchard commended the team for "having a good crack at it."

"They call it the Gabbatoir for a reason, you go there and get absolutely mauled," Mr Pritchard said.

Jimmy Pritchard said seeing Tex Walker walk off the field after his final game was "really emotional". (ABC News: Will Hunter)

Emotional end to Walker's career

Mr Pritchard said he appreciated everything retiring player Tex Walker did for the club, with the veteran completing his 318th and final AFL game on Saturday.

Walker kicked two goals in the last quarter of his career before bidding a tearful goodbye after full-time.

"Tex walking off the field really emotional with the kids, I just really loved that," Mr Pritchard said.

Tony Casiero also wished Walker all the best after a 19-season career.

"I think he should be happy and proud of what he's achieved for our team, for our club, for our state," Mr Casiero said.

"I wish things could've been better for him."

Josh Nacca (right) says there's the potential for the team to be a "real powerhouse" into the future. (ABC News: Will Hunter)

Crushing end

Disappointed fan Josh Nacca said there needed to be some strategic changes in the team to win a premiership.

"The first quarter wasn't good enough, those first five goals really killed the game," he said.

He said the team could be a "real powerhouse" into the future but there were some tough teams to beat.

"Hawthorn, Fremantle, Brisbane, they're looking too strong," he said.

Crows fan Katerina Panayi says she had been optimistic this year. (ABC News: Will Hunter)

Deflated Crows fan Katerina Panayi said she had been optimistic this year.

"I had my flights and accommodation booked for Melbourne, regardless. I was really excited to fight for those grand final tickets," Ms Panayi said.

"I wish I could say next year is the year, but I think we've got a way to go."

title: Breaking: SA records first bird flu case in sea lion
text:
South Australia has recorded its first confirmed detection of H5 bird flu in an Australian sea lion.

SA's Environment Minister Emily Bourke said the sea lion was found at Seal Bay on Kangaroo Island.

The entire sea lion population is estimated to be fewer than 10,000, with 85 per cent in South Australia and the remaining 15 per cent in Western Australia.

Last month, the virus was detected in a long-nosed fur seal in SA's south-east, marking Australia's first positive case in a mammal.

title: PM defends late mother against Hanson public housing 'attack'
text:
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has become emotional defending his late mother against an "attack" by Pauline Hanson, who criticised the time she spent living in public housing.

Mr Albanese has been open about his upbringing in public housing in Sydney's inner west, where his mother Maryanne Albanese raised him by herself.

Speaking to Karl Stefanovic in February, Senator Hanson labelled the repeated references as "pathetic" and said it was "not on" for people like Ms Albanese to live in assisted housing for decades.

"I actually grew up in a street where we had housing commission houses there. It was a helping hand to those people, but they had jobs. And they worked," she told Stefanovic.

"Housing commission houses should not be there for people to live in them for 30, 40 [years] – and he said his mother lived in the same one she was born in for 65 years."

Addressing the resurfaced remarks on Sunday morning, Mr Albanese said he was "stunned" by the attack on his mother, who died in 2002.

"If Pauline Hanson wants to criticise me, then that's fine, but my mother was way out of Pauline Hanson's league, way out of it," he said, his bottom lip quivering.

Anthony Albanese has fondly recalled his kind and nurturing late mother, Maryanne. (Supplied: Instagram)

The prime minister said his mother had a caring nature, despite many health challenges, including severe rheumatoid arthritis, which crippled her joints.

The condition meant she and her son relied on a disability pension.

"She was compassionate, not uncaring. She was generous, not mean, and she was kind, not nasty. She was a person of great character," Mr Albanese said.

"Kindness isn't weakness. Tell you what's weak: nastiness and spitefulness."

He said comments that he complained about growing up in public housing could not be "further from the truth", declaring himself "proud to be a houso".

Calls for Hanson to apologise to PM

Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie criticised Senator Hanson's comments and said mothers should be left out of politics.

Mr Hastie went head-to-head with Senator Hanson this week, demanding she take down a One Nation cartoon branding the veteran a "traitor" after he was hit with a subpoena ordering him to give evidence in a defamation case brought by former SAS corporal Ben Roberts-Smith.

"I think this is another indicator to the Australian people that she's not fit to be prime minister," he told News24.

"I don't think you should be talking about the late mother of anyone in this game."

Andrew Hastie says mothers should be left out of politics. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

Trade Minister Don Farrell labelled the remarks "appalling" and called on Senator Hanson to apologise to Mr Albanese.

"I think it was an inappropriate and appalling comment," he told News24.

"Attacking the prime minister's mother like this is not a way to get respect and dignity from your colleagues, and I think Pauline should reflect upon the attack on the prime minister's mother and withdraw those comments and apologise.

"I don't think there's any other way forward for her over this issue."

title: Warriors moved to Eden Park for Knights finals showdown
text:
The Warriors will make history when they host their first NRL final at Eden Park after the governing body announced the venue for the club's elimination final.

The NRL confirmed the Warriors would play Newcastle at Eden Park next Sunday at 6:05pm (4:05pm AEST) in week two of the finals.

The Warriors' first preference is to play at Mt Smart Stadium where their support is through the roof.

Eden Park holds 50,000 people, however, and is a more modern stadium compared to Mt Smart, where a sold-out crowd of 26,131 created a cauldron-like atmosphere in the Warriors' 26-16 loss to the Dolphins in Saturday night's qualifying final.

The Warriors have hosted five finals in their history in Auckland, but all at Mt Smart.

The Warriors have injury concerns ahead of the clash with the Knights, who they beat 46-32 in Auckland in round 25.

They lost strike centre Leka Halasima in the warm-up to the Dolphins clash with the Tonga international clutching at his right leg.

Trindall returns from shoulder dislocation to lead Sharks in finals win Four weeks after dislocating his shoulder, Braydon Trindall has returned to lead the Cronulla Sharks to a 26-16 win, advancing to the second week of the NRL finals while knocking out the North Queensland Cowboys.

"It was a hamstring in the warm-up, nothing related to what he's been having, which was an ankle injury," coach Andrew Webster said.

"He just felt his hamstring in the first stride out and reported it straight away. Yeah, couldn't go.

"I don't know any more than that right now."

Halasima is set to miss the Newcastle clash amid fears that prop Jackson Ford's injury comeback will be short-lived.

Ford, on return after a 12-week pectoral tear lay-off, limped off against the Dolphins with an ankle complaint.

"Not good," Webster said, when asked about the nature of the injury.

"We don't know much more."

The Warriors were never in full cry in attack against the Dolphins, with five penalty goals edging them to a 16-8 lead, but also denying them the chance near the opposition tryline to perhaps put the game to bed.

"We didn't get the opportunity to get a flow in to our attack," Webster said.

"That's the negative side of taking the penalty goals. But to stretch the lead out to eight points, we had to do it. It's a no-brainer.

"The negative side is there, but the eight-point gap is what every team should take."

Webster said the Warriors were in a strong position when leading 12-8 at half-time, but were unable to contain Dolphins centre Herbie Farnworth in particular as their tackles failed to stick.

"We were trying so hard … chasing contact and collision, and they were pinballing. We have to be more efficient next week."

AAP

title: Immigrants wary of becoming political fodder as migration debate heats up
text:
Barbara Dervodel is grateful for every single day she has lived in Australia.

Ten years ago, she and her husband, Jure, migrated from their native Slovenia.

Settling in Mandurah, a coastal community 70 kilometres south of Perth in Western Australia, the now 34-year-old said the migration process was challenging "but worth every difficult moment".

The couple came to Australia in 2017 after completing their Masters degrees in science. They spent a year on working holiday visas, fell in love with the country and after five years got permanent residency.

"We are proud Australians now," Ms Dervodel said. So too is their two-year-old daughter.

But the happiness she feels is tinged by an unsettling feeling.

She is not alone. Many migrants, who contacted the ABC's Your Say project, feel the same.

They do not want to become political fodder as the two major parties and One Nation squabble over migration numbers.

Loading

American by birth, Australian by choice

Annaliese Claydon was born in America. After 14 years and a long, emotional journey, she became an Australian citizen on Australia Day this year.

"I am an American by birth and an Australian by choice and I would like to do anything I could to help my beloved adopted country avoid sinking into the mire of right-wing nonsense that is tearing my original country apart," she said.

Annaliese Claydon says she is American by birth and Australian by choice. (Supplied: Annaliese Claydon)

"If people knew more about how hard it is to get a visa, how migrants are forced to be separated from their families and elderly parents and how petrifying it is to ask for help when you are on a temporary or a permanent visa, they might think differently about their support for One Nation."

Ms Claydon now lives in Hobart and is a historian and adjunct researcher at the University of Tasmania.

She first came to Australia in 2011 to attend a conference in Sydney, tacked on a side research trip to Hobart and met her now husband there.

Originally from Alaska, she moved to Australia in 2012, applied for a partner visa, married, had a baby and finally, after 14 years, was granted citizenship.

It was, she said, a torturous process during which she endured postpartum depression, struggled without her family but was too scared to ask for help for fear that her visa and residency would be jeopardised.

Watch National Forum on ABC TV and iview David Speers puts the big questions on migration, multiculturalism and national identity to the people shaping the debate on Monday at 8:30pm AEST on ABC TV and ABC iview.

In the context of the current migration debate, she worries about those now in her former position as a temporary resident.

"I worry about people being made to feel like aliens in the homeland they have chosen."

Misinformation and myths

Alan Gamlen, director of the Australian National University's Migration Hub, was blunt: "A lot of the migration debate is being driven by misinformation and myths."

Professor Gamlen said it was a myth that Australia's housing crisis results from excessive migration. He also said it is a myth that migrants are stealing jobs or "lazing around on benefits".

Professor Gamlen argued that we need a better migration debate, informed by an independent arbiter like a national migration institute, and that our politicians are fixated on the wrong number.

"We're talking about net overseas migration (NOM), which is an abstract figure: arrivals minus departures that nobody really understands.

"And political parties are kind of plucking net migration target numbers out of the air without any clear rationale for why their number is better than the other guys," Professor Gamlen said.

What do you want to tell us? Have Your Say Our best stories start with listening to yours. Tell us what Australia should know.

Net overseas migration was 305,000 in 2024-2025, down from 429,000 the previous year but still elevated from pre-COVID NOM of 241,000 in 2018-2019, according to the Australian Government's Institute of Health and Welfare.

The federal government has forecast it to drop to 295,000 for the 2025-2026 financial year.

Professor Gamlen said the NOM was the wrong statistic to focus on.

"If we treat net migration as the problem, we're supporting the false conclusion that all migration is the problem. That is clearly not the case."

Temporary migration

According to Professor Gamlen, the issue is temporary migration — where people are living in Australia on visas, including students, working holiday visas, and temporary skilled workers — and this has "mushroomed", roughly tripling in size after it was deregulated in the early 2000s.

"We have a temporary program where people can come in on one visa and then jump around onto lots of different visas, so we don't really know how long they're going to be in the country. And we don't know if they will ever leave or become permanent," he said.

According to the Department of Home Affairs, the number of people in Australia on temporary visas, including New Zealand citizens, has grown from 1.75m in 2012 to almost 2.9m at the end of July this year.

Alan Gamlen says the migration debate is fixated on the wrong numbers. (ABC: Stuart Carnegie)

However, Professor Gamlen said this number included crew and transit, visitors and New Zealanders, and in an immigration debate, the better comparison excluded those numbers.

He estimated that temporary visa holders excluding these groups had tripled since the early 2000s.

Professor Gamlen said "putting a target on all migration is an extremely blunt instrument" and instead, the country needed a "coherent national population policy" that focuses on regulating the size of the temporary migration program while balancing economic needs and community values.

"In 10 years time, if we get migration policy right … We have a migration program which is large enough to offset our problem of aging, but not too large that it loses social license and makes people feel that the world around them is changing too fast."

Regional migration

Regional Australia Institute CEO Liz Ritchie agreed that planning was key to sustainable population growth, which is vital for regional communities.

New research from the RAI reveals migration accounted for 46.2 per cent of regional population growth in 2025.

The Regional Population Planning report found the largest migrant cohort arriving in regional Australia was aged between 25 and 44, bringing much-needed workers and families to the regions.

The report called for a national regional population settlement strategy.

Liz Ritchie says Australia needs a national settlement strategy. (ABC News: Luke Stephenson)

"Current government projections assume that four in five of the 13.4 million additional Australians expected over the next 40 years will settle in our capital cities," Ms Ritchie said.

"Rather than planning for ever-larger capital cities and a future dominated by megacities, we should be looking at the regional communities that are actively calling for more people and more investment.

"We need a national regional population settlement strategy."

Challenges of moving regional

Settling in regional Australia has been challenging for medical laboratory technician Faris Al-Hilli, who arrived in Australia with his wife and two children in February 2022, on a skilled migrant visa.

Under the system, Mr Al-Hilli had to spend at least two years in a regional area, so the family moved to Murray Bridge, in the Murraylands region of South Australia, about 80km south-east of Adelaide. The town is recognised as a welcoming community for migrants.

Faris Al-Hilli (far right) with his wife Zina and children Ahmed and Samara arrived in Australia from their native Iraq in 2022. (Supplied: Faris Al-Hilli)

But without any local experience he found it difficult to find work in his trained profession in biomedicine and instead worked for just over a year in a mushroom factory. He then worked as a hydrotherapy pool attendant.

Finally, in 2024, he secured a job as a laboratory manager at a local school. For 17 years, in his native Iraq, he had worked as a university tutor and he would love to return to a similar role in the future.

Mr Al-Hilli said the issue he faced as a skilled migrant was the difficulty getting a job without "local" experience.

"It's a contradiction," Mr Al-Hilli said. "I was a little bit surprised. I thought when they accept the skilled immigrant they recognise the skills."

Faris Al-Hilli arrived in Australia in 2022 and lives with his family in the Murraylands region of South Australia. (Supplied: Faris Al-Hilli)

He faced a similar challenge finding a place to rent. Without a rental history the family did not stand a good chance with real estate agents, eventually securing a house directly through an owner.

National regional plan

Ms Ritchie said migration pathways should be a core element of a national plan to support regional communities to attract the workers, skills and families they need to grow.

"If Australia is serious about getting the full benefits of migration, we need a much more deliberate conversation about where new migrants can contribute most, and where communities have the capacity and opportunity to welcome them," she said.

The report argued that directing a greater share of overseas migration to regional Australia could "help address workforce shortages, strengthen local economies and support more sustainable population growth, but only if governments plan for it".

title: Newman Rodeo's return for first time since 2019 draws 'royalty'
text:
Rodeo royalty Ariana Rhodes is among the dozens of competitors who travelled from far and wide to compete in Newman's revitalised rodeo.

Eleven-year-old Ariana and her eight-year-old cousin Svetalina Stones trotted their horses around the red dirt arena that reflects the Pilbara town's mining roots.

The pair appeared at home despite it being somewhat different to where they normally ride in Lake Clifton, south of Perth, 1,200 kilometres away.

Newman, deep in the heartland of iron ore country, has not had a rodeo since 2019.

Royalty at the red dirt rodeo

Crowned Rodeo Mini Princess last year, this is Ariana's first Newman Rodeo.

Rodeo Mini Princess Ariana Rhodes travelled more than 1,000 kilometres for the event.

"I'm competing in barrel racing and pole bending," she said.

"My favourite's barrel racing."

Svetalina hopes to follow in her older cousin's footsteps and did not hesitate when asked about her favourite event.

"Barrel racing," she said with conviction.

Newman was the furthest she had travelled for rodeo.

Svetalina competed in pole bending and barrel racing. (ABC News: Kimberley Putland)

The royal family lived up to their title, taking out medals for their events.

Ariana placed first in her class for barrel racing and pole bending, while Svetalina placed third in barrel racing and second in pole bending.

Talk of the town

Locals warmly welcomed the rodeo's return.

Shire of East Pilbara president Anthony Middleton said Newman had been quietly buzzing in the lead-up to the event.

"There's a fair bit of talk; it hasn't happened since before COVID," he said.

"I didn't realise how important it was to the community … it's exciting to see."

Newman's last rodeo was before COVID in 2019. (ABC News: Kimberley Putland)

Newman Campdraft and Rodeo Association president Cameron Wilson said it was special to bring rodeo back to Newman.

"It's going to be great for the town, great for the people, and just great to see it back in Newman," he said.

Mr Hall believed the turnout would be close to 1,300 people.

Cameron Hall, president of the Newman Campdraft and Rodeo Association, says he hopes the event will become a mainstay of the town. (ABC News: Kimberley Putland)

"I just think it's a great exercise for the town to show what we can produce; obviously, being such a small mining town, we don't have a lot of major events," he said.

" If we can establish this and keep it a recurring thing, I think it's only going to get bigger and better year on year. "

Bringing rodeo back to the Pilbara

Launching Roebourne Rodeo last year, Karlayura Rodeo co-founder Tui Magner said it made sense for Karlayura to bring rodeo back to Newman.

The mining town of Newman had quietly been buzzing in the lead-up to its first rodeo this decade. (ABC News: Kimberley Putland)

"Myself, Brian Tucker and Georgina Bobby have really big dreams to activate rodeos more in the Pilbara," Ms Magner said.

"Doing Roebourne Rodeo in the west Pilbara, now coming over to the east has sort of been a perfect next step to build on that success.

"Newman itself has quite a long history in rodeo … we're just really trying to build on that success."

Tui Magner, co-founder of Karlayura Rodeo. (ABC News: Kimberley Putland)

Competitors from as far north as the Kimberley region and as far away as the South West travelled for the full-points event.

Fellow Karlayura co-founder Georgina Bobby said Newman held a special place in the Karlayura team's heart.

"This place is in Nyiyiparli country, which is Brian Tucker's mother's homeland," she said.

"I think he wanted to bring it back here for his people."

Georgina Bobby is another co-founder of Karlayura Rodeo. (ABC News: Kimberley Putland)

Ms Bobby highlighted the relationship between Aboriginal stockmen and modern-day rodeo.

"Back in the day, the elders, old people then, they pretty much worked on stations," she said.

"It'll be good for them to see something that's come back with this rodeo, recognising those people."

title: Root says England's back from 'chaos' after Pakistan series sweep
text:
Joe Root admits England descended into "chaos" before he returned as the Test captain and believes things are back on track after sealing a cricket series whitewash over Pakistan on Saturday.

England survived a scare before Root and Jordan Cox scored unbeaten half-centuries to knock off the target of 130 and win the third Test at Edgbaston by eight wickets with five sessions to spare.

The dramatic retirement of Ben Stokes in June followed by coach Brendon McCullum being stripped of his red-ball responsibilities briefly left the Test side with a worrying leadership vacuum.

Root, who served as skipper for five years before standing down in 2022, accepted the captaincy again and, in concert with interim coach Marcus Trescothick, brought a hat-trick of comfortable wins at Leeds, Lord's and now Edgbaston.

The partnership steadied the ship ahead of Stephen Fleming's arrival as McCullum's long-term successor.

The Kiwi is due to arrive in the country in the coming days and Root believes he will find a team that has put its turbulent recent past to one side.

"There's been a lot of chaos around this series before a ball was bowled," Root said.

"The way we've handled it on and off the field, the way everyone understands what is expected of them, both as a player and how we want to carry ourselves, is a really good thing.

"It's been a very unusual summer, hasn't it? We had a resignation mid-series, there has been a few off-field incidents and we've got a new coach. Whether you call it chaos, whether you call it unusual, whether you call it unsettling, all of those are fair.

Root fuming after Carse nightclub incident England captain Joe Root opens up on his disappointment after finding another teammate involved in an alcohol-fuelled off-field incident.

"But ultimately, the thing that I care about and the most important thing is what happens from that. The way that we've responded to that has been excellent. And the fact that there's now clarity in what is expected of the group moving forward is quite evident. We build on that now."

Pakistan finally put England under some pressure in Birmingham after flaccid efforts in the first two games.

A stunning 81-run cameo from debutant Razaullah Khan on Friday left England chasing 130.

In Saturday's first over, the host was reduced to 2-2 when Mohammad Abbas got Ben Duckett to edge behind and Emilio Gay lbw.

"We thought this morning that anything is possible," Abbas said. "My specialty is taking wickets with the new ball … and we tried our best."

England could have been 3-35 when Root dragged on but Mohammad Ali overstepped.

Root and Cox shared an unbeaten stand of 128 with Root finishing on 62 and Cox 59 when they won at 2-133 just before lunch.

Seam bowler Ollie Robinson was named the player of the series for taking 21 wickets at an average of 8.76.

title: When Charlie isn't at school, he's welding thousand dollar scrap sculptures
text:
Before Dunsborough teenager Charlie Guiver could walk, his parents were teaching him to use his own electric drill.

The 14-year-old has since honed his craft as a sculptor using scrap metal, recently selling one of his pieces, a large wolf sculpture, for $8,000.

Juggling school and homework, he spends all his spare time on weekends and evenings beavering away on his animal creations.

"It's just fun going into the workshop and cutting up tools and then fitting them into place, a bit like a puzzle," he said.

Charlie Guiver spends all his spare time working in his Dunsborough studio. (ABC News: Mietta Adams)

Charlie sources his materials from local salvage yards to create the sculptures, with his favourite a kinetic eagle which he designed to swing with the wind.

"Before I start a sculpture, I know how I'm going to make it in my head, then I just go out and find the tools and weld it all together," he said.

Charlie Guiver's favourite piece is a kinetic eagle which moves with the wind. (ABC News: Mietta Adams)

Opening studio to public

Charlie will offer the public a behind-the-scenes glimpse into his creative process, opening his shed studio for the first time as part of the Margaret River Region Open Studios event.

He is the youngest artist to participate in the show, which is the largest of its kind in the country with 155 artists opening their doors for two weeks from September 12.

Charlie was given his first drill at two years old. (ABC News: Mietta Adams)

Charlie said his dream is to travel to Europe with his older brother to learn about traditional blacksmithing techniques.

"I don't know if it will ever be a career but I will always do it as a hobby," he said.

His mother Kath Guiver said he has always been interested in taking apart and re-making toys and is "very proud" of his artwork.

"It's hard to reconcile the age he is because he comes out and does these amazing things," she said.

Loading

End of an era

As Charlie prepares to share his studio for the first time, it will be the last time Margaret River glass artist Gerry Reilly will open his studio to the public.

Gerry Reilly uses a kiln heated to 1,100 degrees Celsius for his glass creations. (ABC News: Mietta Adams)

Having operated as an open studio seven days a week since 1991 and participating in the region's open studio event since its inception 13 years ago, it is with mixed feelings he prepares to close the kiln.

"I'm at an area in my career now where I've made objects and studied for 50 years and I might step back from it a little bit for a while and just see what else evolves into that space," he said.

"I'm kind of looking forward to having a break, but I've also got some trepidation about what I'm going to do with my time next."

Some of Gerry Reilly's creations on display at his Melting Pot Glass Studio in Margaret River. (ABC News: Mietta Adams)

He said the event attracts people to the Margaret River region from across the state and the country to learn about the skills involved in glass blowing.

"If people just see your stuff in the gallery, they might wonder how it's done. But here they can see and explore it themselves," he said.

Gerry Reilly, with partner Margot Edwards at their studio in Margaret River. (ABC News: Mietta Adams)

Meanwhile for the artists, Reilly said it is an important opportunity to present their work and boost sales after the quieter winter period.

Last year, the event attracted more than 100,000 studio visits and generated more than $2 million in art sales.

The event runs until September 27.

title: Women say outback contest 'not just bikinis and beauty'
text:
Francisca Henriquez never thought she'd be walking down a catwalk in outback Western Australia.

The 31-year-old, recently crowned 2026 Miss Cable Beach, said she was naturally a shy person.

Ms Henriquez said hearing her friends cheer from the crowd brought out her "alter ego". (Supplied: Divers Tavern)

But gliding down a pub stage in front of a packed crowd in Broome brought out her "alter ego".

"All my friends, all the people I love were there to support me and scream my name," she said.

"I really love that energy around me."

The Miss Cable Beach contest has been running for more than three decades, and continues to draw crowds and numerous entries.

Miss Cable Beach first launched at Divers Tavern in 1991. (Supplied: Divers Tavern)

While core aspects of the competition have held firm, organisers argue the event has evolved since its 1991 inception.

Events coordinator at Divers Tavern Saoirse Meally said participants were given more opportunities to share their personality and style, with the addition of more questions and a resort wear round.

"It's not just all about the bikini and appearance, it's about what's inside the girl too," she said.

Ms Meally said the competition had evolved to be more than "appearance and bikinis". (ABC Kimberley: Rachel Jackson)

" Girls of every shape and size can get on that stage. "

Ms Meally said she had seen women "completely come out of their shells" after competing.

"After they've done it, they're on a high for a week," she said.

"Their perception of it completely changes."

Hailing from Chile, Ms Henriquez has called Broome home for four years.

She first entered last year with hopes of purchasing her mother a plane ticket to Broome using the $10,000 prize money.

Ms Henriquez said she was surprised by the contest's welcoming environment. (Supplied: Divers Tavern)

The contest surprised her.

"For sure it's about beauty, but also something deeper about how women feel about themselves," she said.

" How they can go on stage and say, 'this is my body and I'm proud about it'. "

While the money might have spurred her entry, Ms Henriquez said it was something she would look back on in years to come.

"I can see how proud I feel about myself," she said.

She said this year's prize money will go towards her next visa application, and dream of staying in town.

For men looking to strut their stuff, a "Mr Cable Beach" event runs alongside the women's final event.

A Mr Cable Beach competition runs alongside the women's final event. (Supplied: Divers Tavern)

Body positive or objectification?

Across Australia, the landscape of bikini competitions has shifted away from casual pub contests to competitive fitness events.

But in Broome, traditions like Miss Cable Beach and the Roebuck Bay Hotel's Wet Tee competition have remained.

Some feel conflicted as to whether these events still have a place in today's society.

The event remains a hit in Broome. (Supplied: Divers Tavern)

Professor of Body Image and Health at Flinders University Ivanka Prichard said her immediate thought when it came to a bikini contest was one of concern.

"Given that a bikini competition would imply that someone's body is on display, potentially objectified," she said.

" We know that when we objectify, particularly the female body, that people feel worse about themselves. "

Professor Prichard said she had a mixed opinion on the events.

"But if it's done carefully and there are a range of options for those competing, then I think that could be a positive thing," she said.

title: No music teacher until high school? This charity fills the gap
text:
Music class at Taree Public School has become one of the reasons the children want to come to school.

After learning to play drums and read music, year 6 student Cooper Hamilton-Riley enjoys the challenge of creating a beat with both hands and feet.

"[It] just feels fun to hit the drums hard and makes me really focus on one thing," Cooper said

Cooper is a proud Biripi boy and plays the drums for the school band. (ABC Mid North Coast: Wiriya Sati)

Cooper and his classmates at the school take part in once-a-week, curriculum-based music session run by Matt Zarb from the not-for-profit, Australian Children's Music Foundation (ACMF).

In New South Wales, public schools don't have a dedicated music teacher before year 7.

"That's like saying I'm going to teach you to read when you're 13," Mr Zarb said.

"All these little children who've got so much music in them with no opportunity."

The ACMF supplies the instruments for their classes targeted at students at regional, remote and disadvantaged primary schools

The project is funded by a mixture of philanthropy and fundraising.

Mr Zarb worked with Cooper's class to harness their musical talent to write a song and film clip that showcased Biripi culture.

"It makes me feel stronger about my culture and happy to be Biripi and Aboriginal," Cooper said.

The school's Aboriginal Education Officer, Toni Baxter, who worked on the cultural dance, language and traditional dress, said the project has brought confidence and pride.

"I've just seen the difference when they first started they were very shy and as we kept coming together they felt comfortable and their confidence just grew."

Taree Public School has a dedicated music room for its weekly visit from ACMF's Matt Zarb. (ABC Mid North Coast: Wiriya Sati)

The ACMF's music program at Kempsey South Public School saw a 13.6 per cent increase in student attendance between 2022 to 2024.

ACMF made a submission to a NSW parliamentary inquiry in 2024 that examined inequity of music education in primary schools, the benefits of quality music education, the resourcing challenges and potential solutions.

The state government response made 30 recommendations to deliver over 10 years between 2025 and 2035.

Some of the recommendations include introducing arts and music specialisation in initial primary school teacher education, and funding development to upskill teachers to have the confidence to deliver music in the syllabus.

The also proposed building further partnerships between artists and musicians and external arts organisations and schools, as well as increasing funds for outside organisations to deliver education and training for teachers.

In a statement, Deputy Premier and Minister for Education and Early Learning Prue Carr said the 10-year plan for music education in public primary schools would be released in the coming weeks.

Matt Zarb provides a band experience for his music students, showing them how to write a song and perform it. (ABC Mid North Coast: Wiriya Sati)

Music helps the brain develop

Anita Collins, a neuro-musical educator and consultant and adjunct associate professor at the University of Canberra, said research showed learning music improved the brain's ability to learn.

"As soon as you do music you're actually improving the pathway for language," Dr Collins said.

"It also improves many parts we then apply to numeracy — it's an area called the abstract thinking network — and mathematics is one of those."

She said the education system nationally needs to ensure all students have access to quality music education.

"There are so many not-for-profits and they're doing an excellent job and they're bringing their expertise to schools and to generalist teachers who've never learnt a musical instrument.

" But we shouldn't be relying on not-for-profits to fill a gap that should be filled by the education system. "

Matt Zarb also works with teachers on ways to deliver simple musicology in the curriculum, in a creative way rather than relying on videos.

"I would love to see myself out of a job," he said.

If there isn't funding for a music teacher, he said, a solution would be to employ a music and creative arts teacher to cover three schools, or a full-time job to cover the whole school of 500 kids.

AEO Toni Baxter and the elders created a cultural dance at their sacred lagoon, Saltwater, as part of the Biripi Song project. (Supplied: Taree Public School)

For now, Taree Public School principal Di Murray said the ACMF was vital to ensuring her students got a comprehensive music education.

Ms Murray said their generalist teachers could deliver the required music curriculum, but it made a difference having a professional musician come in.

"The difference is here you have Matty who just has this love of music, he's a performer, he's so animated in his teaching and just motivates not only the students but the teachers as well," she said.

" I just like to think that every child gets the musical experience that our kids do, whether it's through ACMF or a teacher that has that skill that goes around to each classroom. "

She said attendance had "improved immensely" since the ACMF program began at Taree Public in 2014, matching the state average at times which was 90 per cent in September 2024.

Matt Zarb said if a child was happy, they would learn well.

"If the kids are getting a chance to experience, read and play music, sing … their whole existence is better at school."

title: New world number one Rybakina dethrones Sabalenka in US Open final
text:
Elena Rybakina has won her first US Open title, ending Aryna Sabalenka's hopes of a hat-trick of wins at Flushing Meadows in New York.

Rybakina controlled the first set, then was put in danger in the second, defending two set points before losing a third to allow Sabalenka back into the match.

However, the Kazakh player held her nerve, taking an early break in the third set and holding on for her third major title win, 6-4, 5-7, 6-2.

The win marked a second major triumph for Rybakina this year, after her Australian Open final victory over Sabalenka in January.

Sabalenka's loss ended her hopes of winning a third US Open crown in a row, emulating tennis great Serena Williams, who was undefeated between 2012 and 2014.

Sabalenka was increasingly frustrated through the match, smashing a couple of racquets as she struggled to find a way past her opponent.

Aryna Sabalenka's inability to crack Elena Rybakina left her frustrated at the US Open final. (Getty Images: Sarah Stier)

Rybakina stopped Sabalenka's 19-match winning streak at the US Open, where she had not lost since falling to Coco Gauff in the 2023 final.

The WTA Tour leader in aces got less than half of her first serves in but instead put Sabalenka under constant pressure with a strong return game, racking up 12 break chances and converting three, which was all she needed.

Rybakina earned $US5.5 million ($7.67 million), the largest prize in grand slam history, and tied Sabalenka and French Open winner Mirra Andreeva with a tour-high three titles this season.

Sabalenka took home $US2.8 million ($3.9 million) but it was clear how little that meant to her, as she smashed her racquet after a brief hug with Rybakina at the net.

A devastated Sabalenka found it hard to talk at the trophy presentation.

"That's the last thing I want to do now is giving a speech," she said.

"Obviously, I'm disappointed but I want to say congratulations Elena, it's a great win.

"I wish I could perform a little better, but maybe next year," she said as tears fell.

Rybakina was overjoyed and a little overwhelmed.

"It's tough to find words right now," she told the crowd.

"I didn't expect anything like this coming to this tournament. I've been dealing with an injury but somehow everything aligned together on my side.

"I want to say to Aryna, you are a great champion. It's so difficult to play you. I was diving around on court trying to get balls [back]."

Rybakina also thanked the crowd for their support, adding: "I'm falling in love with New York more and more."

It was celebration time for Elena Rybakina at the US Open after she won her second major title of 2026. (Getty Images: Julian Finney)

The second seed drew first blood to go ahead 3-2 following a Sabalenka double ⁠fault, with the frustrated Belarusian earning a code ‌violation immediately afterwards for launching ‌a ball high into the stands of the main showcourt.

A sudden drop-off in Rybakina's level midway through the second set gave the 28-year-old Sabalenka hope, and she produced a delicate drop shot and a stunning backhand crosscourt winner en route to forcing a deciding set.

However, Rybakina's quality ‌shone through as she took a commanding 5-2 lead and then ​closed out a famous triumph to leave her Belarusian rival without any major silverware in 2026.

title: Former fire station crucial to Men's Shed faces government sell-off
text:
In a secluded pocket of northern Tasmanian bushland, restoring a disused section of railway has become a passion project for dozens of volunteers.

Crucial to the Launceston and North East Railway group's operations is a former country fire station, which was in a "neglected" state when the group became primary caretakers of the property in 2022.

But it was just what they were looking for.

The Karoola fire station has been maintained by the railway group and Men's Shed since 2022. (ABC News)

The group, which is also a registered Men's Shed, has restored and maintained the decommissioned Karoola fire station for the past four years.

"It's been crucial for our activities," said Launceston and North East Railway (L&NER) chair Elizabeth Cute.

" We've made projects and done things because we've had the facilities, whereas we haven't previously. "

Volunteers have helped maintain the station's surroundings for years. (Facebook: Launceston and North East Railway)

Now, the group's "devastated and distressed" members fear their entire mission is in jeopardy amid a government plan to sell the decommissioned fire station.

'No formal agreement' in place

On July 7, Fire and Emergency Services Commissioner Jeremy Smith wrote to Ms Cute regarding the Karoola fire station.

"The State Fire Commission (SFC), which owns the property, has determined that the site is surplus to operational requirements and approved the disposal of the Karoola Fire Station through a public sale process," he said.

" This ensures the sale is conducted in a transparent and equitable manner and achieves an appropriate market return. "

Elizabeth Cute says the Tasmania Fire Service has backflipped on a longstanding verbal agreement. (ABC News: Hayden Smith)

Commissioner Smith said the group would be allowed to use the site until it was sold.

Ms Cute said the "huge blow" was in stark contrast to a "verbal agreement" the group had struck with the Tasmania Fire Service (TFS).

"They basically gave us the intention that they were going to give us the fire station down the track because they didn't need it," she told the ABC.

" Your word used to be your honour, but it obviously is not. "

Ms Cute believed the department was focusing purely on the bottom line amid sweeping cuts to the Tasmanian public service.

Brian McKenna is among the group's growing list of members. (ABC News: Hayden Smith)

A Department of Police, Fire and Emergency Management spokesperson said that, since 2022, L&NER and Men's Shed had "used the site informally and at no cost".

"While TFS initially considered a lease arrangement, no formal agreement was established," they said.

"L&NER has expressed a preference to remain at the site and has been encouraged to participate in the sale process."

However, Ms Cute said the group was not in a financial position to purchase the site.

The government says "no formal agreement was established" over the future use of the station. (Facebook: Launceston and North East Railway)

Morale low but fight continues

For longstanding members such as Greg Stewart, losing access to the site is tough to accept.

The L&NER vice-chair was instrumental in starting a new pedal-powered rail bug venture, which has been operational since May this year.

"For me it's devastating," he said.

" We built the whole thing on this being a permanent hub. "

Greg Stewart fears the rail bug operation will cease to operate. (ABC Northern Tasmania: Sarah Abbott)

Mr Stewart said he would love to sit down with the TFS and politicians for a "commonsense chat".

"The gain for the community from this shed is so much more than selling it," he said.

Ms Cute said morale among members was low.

title: Devastating, funny, heartbreaking and hopeful – RECLAIM was one of the best dance events in years
text:
State Library of NSW, September 11

The Mitchell Library’s colonial splendour is wreathed in ceremonial smoke when I arrive: ornate moulded walls, towering bookshelves, spiral stairs leading to elevated balconies and soaring skylights crowning a vast central reading space.

Here, amid the books, drawers, and antique reading tables, dance legend Stephen Page is back with a site-specific premiere. The former Bangarra Dance Theatre artistic director wields his fellowship with the State Library of NSW in RECLAIM: A Contemporary Ceremony, co-written with Alana Valentine for the library’s 200th anniversary.

A scene from RECLAIM: A Contemporary Ceremony, co-written by Stephen Page with Alana Valentine at the State Library of NSW for the library’s 200th anniversary. Daniel Boud

Damien Cooper’s stage lights illuminate and the shelves seem to fade under fingers of sunlight and tree branches, the plasterwork receding beneath lapping coastal waves. The air comes alive with Steve Francis’s soundscape of birds, crackling fire and haunting Indigenous song, joined by the plaintive strains of Taj Pigram’s voice and mandolin.

The performers sweep onstage in ceremonial dance, singing and bearing leaves as light rays fall behind them like a setting sun. The impact is immediate, uncanny and unspeakably beautiful: the library’s familiar architecture superimposed with an overwhelming evocation of Country and memory. It is like being gifted second sight, the library fracturing into palpable layers of time and meaning before your eyes, each layer simultaneously visible and powerful.

In Protest, actors Brendon Boney, Angeline Penrith and Dalara Williams trace the work of generations of Indigenous advocates. Daniel Boud

Seven scenes follow, the audience gazing through the centuries at a crescendo of storytelling: by turns warm, devastating, funny, heartbreaking and hopeful.

In Place, Indigenous engagement librarian Melissa Jackson speaks from a balcony about the library’s decolonisation work, followed by Bradley Smith’s searing solo as an Indigenous man reduced to a collected “specimen”.

A scene from the work, which was warm, devastating, funny, heartbreaking and hopeful. Daniel Boud

In Protest, actors Brendon Boney, Angeline Penrith and Dalara Williams in early 20th-century costume (Jennifer Irwin’s designs) are assembled beneath a banner, megaphone in hand, tracing generations of Indigenous advocates. Their true stories will make your eyes sting with tears.

An excerpt from Page’s Patyegarang pairs Smith and Buia David in a gorgeously romantic duet about the first historical colonial-Indigenous exchange of Dharug language. Preen has Penrith comically auditioning to play Matthew Flinders’ cat; and Protect warms with a storytelling tribute to Mum Shirl.

The evening emotionally detonates with Presence, the devastating final scene from Page’s Bennelong. The stage blazes with Beau Dean Riley Smith, reprising the eponymous role he originated, his electric limbs seemingly thrown together and torn apart by tectonic external forces, his face caught between surprise and pain. The concluding image – Riley Smith crying out as he is walled up alive in a white sepulchre – is every bit as poetic and horrifying as at its premiere almost a decade ago.

Somehow, these vignettes never feel like a Page jukebox. Page turns his extraordinary body of work into another kind of archive, placing past choreography beside living testimony, new theatrical scenes, historical storytelling, and the library’s own collection until each illuminates the others. RECLAIM is site-specific work in the fullest sense: it changes how you see the building itself.

At the finish, the audience leaps to its feet with a roar. Unmissable, and one of the best dance events in years.

It’s been 15 long years, but the Wests Tigers are finally playing finals football again. For the first time since 2011, a top-grade Tigers team will play a match at the business end of the season, thanks to the club’s NRLW side sealing a top-four finish with a 7-4 record during the 11-match regular season. Wests Tigers captain Kezie Apps has been with the team since their inaugural year in 2022. George Chan It’s an impressive turnaround for a team that finished with just one win, and the wooden spoon for the second year in a row in 2025. The last Wests Tigers team to play finals was Tim Sheen’s 2011 squad that included Marshall, Lote Tuqiri and Robbie Farah.

Advertisement

One of the most significant changes for the NRLW team this year has been the arrival of coach Craig Sandercock. “If you were to say to me at the start of the year, you’re playing finals footy, I would have 100 per cent taken that,” Sandercock said. Wests Tigers NRLW coach Craig Sandercock. NRL Images “It’s been a great, great year, and you could probably consider it a really successful year from the club, especially with where we’ve come from.” The team always had potential, said Sandercock, but there were a handful of areas that required improvement.

“When I watched all their games from last year, they only won one game, but there were periods in every game that they competed, and they competed hard, and it was just, I suppose, some key moments last year that really cost them,” Sandercock said. “Then that fed into that mindset of, here we go again, and then they concede another try and another try. So, for us, it was all about trying to build some resilience and really work hard on icing or winning those key moments in games that can lead to positive results.” The recruitment of veteran players Raecene McGregor and Shaylee Bent has also been a huge boost, and those experienced players have joined forces with captain Kezie Apps and forward Sarah Togatuki – who have been with the club since that first 2023 season – to steer the team into the finals. “I feel like this year the coach and the recruitment [team] have done a great job of finding that balance [between youth an experience],” said Apps.

“We’ve still got our young girls coming through who are learning and who are going really good, but we’ve also got that great balance of the leaders and the experience within the group as well. “It’s obviously been a big change this year from going from only winning one game last year, and now here we are near finals, and we’ve come fourth. “Reflecting on the season that we’ve had ... and comparing that to last year coming last and then coming fourth, I think that’s something that needs to be celebrated and something that needs to be recognised of how hard the girls have worked to get to where we are.” The Tigers will play either Newcastle, who they beat with a 68th-minute field goal in round eight, or Canberra, who they lost 22-10 to in the final round of the season, in week one of the finals.

Cronulla chief executive Dino Mezzatesta fears the Sharks may never host an NRL final in their own backyard again, but says the NRL should implement a blanket finals policy that will ensure all clubs are treated the same. The Sharks’ 26-16 defeat of North Queensland at Allianz Stadium was attended by an official crowd of 17,429 on Saturday night, only around 2500 more than the capacity of Cronulla’s regular home ground, Ocean Protect Stadium. Loading Under discretionary powers outlined to NRL clubs at the start of the season, the ARLC retains the right to decide where week one finals are played, chiefly to ensure fans aren’t locked out of smaller venues like Sydney’s boutique stadiums. The NRL opted to move the qualifying final between the Sharks and the Cowboys to Allianz Stadium, but the underwhelming crowd on Saturday prompted yet another round of debate around the Cronulla club’s right to host finals.

Star halfback Nicho Hynes appeared to question the NRL’s decision to shift the game, telling Channel Nine that while he was not blaming Sharks fans, he found it “upsetting, disappointing and embarrassing there’s so many free seats here”. Mezzatesta and Sharks officials have stridently argued for Cronulla’s earned right to host a home final in the Shire over several recent seasons. North Queensland’s Braidon Burns scores in front of plenty of empty seats at Allianz Stadium. Getty Images But given the NRL’s decision to move Saturday’s match against the traditionally low-drawing out-of-town Cowboys to Moore Park, Mezzatesta responded to the modest crowd by calling on the governing body to now make it a level playing field and scrap the discretionary aspect. “I’m still disappointed because nothing will change the fact that we earned the right to play that home semi-final at our home ground,” Mezzatesta said on Sunday.

Advertisement

“But maybe we’re at the point where you have to change that rule for everyone then. Just play the semis at all the big stadiums from here on, regardless of who is in. “If you’re a Sydney team, you’re playing at Allianz, Accor [Stadium] or Commbank [Stadium]. If you’re in Queensland, you play at Suncorp [Stadium] and if you’re in New Zealand, then you play at Eden [Park]. Ocean Protect Stadium has various issues holding it back from hosting NRL finals. Harry Breen “I don’t mean to disadvantage other clubs, but we have this discussion every year around finals venues every year, and to me, if you’re not going to let us play at our home ground, then lock in the big venues and take the guessing games and the controversy out of it.” Mezzatesta’s suggestion would mean Sydney clubs like Manly (Four Pines Park), St George Illawarra (Kogarah and WIN Stadium) and Wests Tigers (Leichhardt Oval and Campbelltown Stadium) would also not have the ability to play finals at their suburban home grounds.

The NRL on Sunday announced that next week’s Warriors-Knights semi-final will be played at Auckland’s Eden Park, which can accommodate around 24,000 more supporters than Go Media Stadium. Given the NRL collects gate takings of all finals matches, at an average of $50 per finals ticket, that represents a windfall of around $1.5 million for the governing body. Warriors fans have good reason to be in full voice this year. Getty Despite the Warriors selling out their surprise week-one loss to the Dolphins in a reported 17 minutes last week, the NRL’s two finals crowds at Allianz Stadium have underwhelmed after another year of strong attendances. South Sydney’s first post-season game since 2022 against the Knights on Friday night drew only 28,152, while the Sharks-Cowboys clash amounted to less than half the venue’s seats being filled.

The presence of big-drawing clubs Canterbury and Brisbane made for bumper crowds and eight of nine finals games being sold out last season (albeit with Shark Park one of those). As for the Sharks, Mezzatesta believes there is still scope to host a home final against interstate opposition rivals like the Cowboys or Titans next year – if the ARLC’s discretionary rules remain. But until Ocean Protect Stadium gets a much-needed upgrade to improve its tired facilities, even that prospect appears slim.

“There’s still a place for suburban grounds in our game,” he said. “We know our facilities need improvements, and we will continue to pursue government funding and Peter V’landys is a big supporter of us doing that. “And once the stadium is back fully online with a capacity of 18,000, well, the discussion around finals changes again. title: Phil wanted to rent a shop in Footscray. The owner would rather it sits empty
text:

Exclusive NationalVictoriaGo west Phil wanted to rent a shop in Footscray. The owner would rather it sits empty Cassandra Morgan September 13, 2026 — 1:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

During five years’ trading in Melbourne’s west, Phil Gaby’s business has had just as many homes. Nan’s Bakehouse began at the markets, then moved to Footscray Plaza before expanding into the business next door. A coffee van followed, then a new store in Moonee Ponds – before its closure, when they ran into financial strife. Nan’s Bakehouse owner Phil Gaby said many landlords in the area would rather keep their shops vacant than have them occupied by businesses. Chris Hopkins Despite failure and two evictions, Nan’s endures in Footscray – one of Melbourne’s toughest places for businesses to thrive, a new Property Council of Australia report suggests. But Gaby said he wouldn’t want to be anywhere else.

Advertisement

“After we failed at Moonee Ponds, I realised that success meant the community and the people,” he said. “Even our store now has been held together by people from our old store, continually following us around because they believe in the same things we do.” The Nicholson Street Mall in Footscray, which is home to the former Forges site, alongside many vacant shopfronts. Joe Armao Despite a $1.5 billion investment in the new Footscray Hospital – and millions more in transport, education, and sporting and social infrastructure – the inner-city suburb has stalled, the Property Council found in its Revitalising Victoria’s priority precincts report, in large part due to land banking. “I applied for one place on Barkly Street, and it has been empty for two years now … The owner said he did not want to spend any money, and he’d rather leave it sitting empty,” Gaby said.

Advertisement

Related Article Go west This western suburb is ripe for a housing boom, council says. Developers disagree “He was concerned that, if the business went bad, then that’s his loss. That’s how he looked at it. Whereas before, a landlord would look at it as an investment.” Footscray’s land banking issue is symptomatic of a more complex problem, whereby high construction costs, elevated taxes and charges, expensive finance and subdued apartment values are deterring landowners from developing projects, the Property Council found. New apartments in Footscray average $100,000 less than Melbourne’s median apartment price, making it difficult for developers to justify new builds when construction costs remain high, KPMG urban economist Terry Rawnsley said. High costs were also accompanied by a 1297 per cent increase in approved dwellings in central Footscray in the 2022-23 financial year, compared with the previous year (908 dwellings from 65).

Advertisement

A similar pattern emerged in the 2024-25 financial year (with 704 approved dwellings, compared to the previous year’s 38), helping to keep prices down. Related Article City life Violence, nostalgia and the unravelling of Melbourne’s first pedestrian mall The Property Council suggests that if prices continue to fall with federal tax changes, this could be replicated across Melbourne and undermine the feasibility of new projects. “Developers are likely to be holding sites and waiting for feasibility to improve,” Rawnsley told The Age. “That could come through stronger sale prices, as the existing apartment supply is absorbed, although there is little indication that construction costs will fall materially in the foreseeable future.”

Advertisement

However, the report warns a “business-as-usual” approach, even with continued local and state government investment, won’t be enough to fix the issues in Footscray. “Getting Footscray right would not only unlock a major opportunity for Melbourne’s west,” Property Council Victorian executive director Cath Evans said. “It could provide a blueprint for how Victoria can turn its broader activity centre and precinct ambitions into reality.” The former Forges site at Nicholson Street Mall in Footscray. Joe Armao The Property Council is urging the state government to commit to a six-step plan to haul Footscray out of its slump, pointing to vacant shopfronts, deteriorating buildings and “hoarded” development sites. The council names the former Forges site, Little Saigon Market, Paint Spot, Kinnear’s Ropeworks, the former bus depot and the former Belgravia Hotel among them, and notes each has their own “commercial circumstances” – but they collectively represent “a significant volume of unrealised housing, employment, activation and public realm challenges”.

Advertisement

At a forum in Footscray making the case for Maribyrnong City Council’s $148 million Creative West arts precinct project last month, Mayor Mohamed Semra described the former Forges site as a once-thriving retail destination, since “left to decay for 17 years”. The report suggests more should be done to capitalise on the arts precinct project, as well as other investments. Related Article City life The old hospital that’s become a battleground in Melbourne’s west The Property Council encouraged government to prioritise improving Footscray’s streetscapes and begin demolition programs to remove derelict or condemned buildings. The state government should also look at waving or reducing taxes and levies for developers building in Footscray and other Melbourne activity centres, tying incentives to timelines or community infrastructure, the Property Council said.

Advertisement

Government should also consider public-private partnerships for big development sites, dedicate a department or area of council to getting a move on big projects, and better coordinate local support services to shore up faith in Footscray’s safety, the report said. Semra said Maribyrnong Council was working to improve Footscray’s safety, amenity and shopfronts, support economic development, and draw people to local attractions and events. He said his council would consider the Property Council’s report. “We’re working collaboratively with landowners, businesses, community organisations, and state and federal governments to speed up action on vacant sites in the Footscray CBD.” The Victorian government pointed to its investment in Footscray’s health, education, transport, sport and community infrastructure. A government spokesperson said that “through planning certainty, infrastructure investment and better transport connections”, the government was helping unlock the area’s growth.
