title: Why young filmmakers are spending their savings on feature films
text:
Advertisement

CultureMoviesCinema Why young filmmakers are spending their savings on feature films Garry Maddox September 13, 2026 — 1:06pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

They are feature films you will almost certainly never see. Made for comically small budgets. Starring no-one you know. Yet at a time when even well-funded Australian films regularly struggle to find an audience, young filmmakers keep making ultra-low budget features, even if it means using up their savings, going into debt and burning favours from friends and acquaintances. “It was always probably my biggest dream to just be in a movie” said actor-writer-director Jonah Erofeyeff (left) with actor Madeleine Walker and actor-writer-director Emrah Akbulut, who made the feature film Where The Sky Meets The Ground for $15,000. Sitthixay Ditthavong Many will never make another film. So why do it? “It was always probably my biggest dream to just be in a movie,” Jonah Erofeyeff, 21, says. “You look up on the big screen and sort of see yourself there.”

Advertisement

Related Article Cinema Armie Hammer is back after being cancelled. But his choice of film is problematic He was not just thinking about himself. Erofeyeff made Where The Sky Meets The Ground with close friend Emrah Akbulut, 21, after meeting at an acting course. It’s a drama about four friends who have one last adventure before uni finishes – trekking into the bush to find a crashed plane supposedly carrying drugs. Akbulut was watching the ’80s classic Stand By Me one night when he realised he had shared similar friendships. Inspired by Stand By Me: Jonah Erofeyeff and Emrah Akbulut’s film Where The Sky Meets The Ground Mach 10

Advertisement

“I messaged Jonah as the credits were rolling, and I was like, ‘This is a movie we can make – modernise it and make it Australian, authentic to us’,” he says. Adds Erofeyeff: “We’re both actors. We wanted to just make a project for us to act in – a feature film with heaps of scenes.” So the duo made the film – jointly writing, directing, starring and financing it – with $15,000 of their savings. Erofeyeff was working in maintenance at theme park Raging Waters (now Sydney Action Park); Akbulut was packaging wool in a warehouse before moving into baggage handling at Sydney Airport. They kept down costs on the shoot by calling on friends from their acting classes and Erofeyeff’s filmmaking course at Randwick TAFE for the cast and crew, car pooling to set and bringing snack bags for everyone. “Should I put a deposit on a house or should I make a film?“: Adrian Ortega largely self-funded the feature film Westgate, with Sarah Nicolazzo, who plays a single mother still carrying trauma from the bridge collapse in 1970. Simon Schluter

Advertisement

When their film was knocked back by festivals and distributors, the duo paid for their own premiere at the Randwick Ritz, gambling – successfully as it turned out – that they could cover the $5000 cost with ticket sales. They are now hoping to make another film. “The main dream is acting, but we always have that drive to make something else,” Akbulut says. “Even if it’s not a full production, we just want to be behind the camera, in front of the camera, doing something.” Sarah Nicolazzo and Max Nappo in Adrian Ortega’s Westgate. Proud Wing Melbourne editor and filmmaking teacher Adrian Ortega was 25 when he shot his first feature film, the comic drama Cerulean Blue, about an introvert (Jack Michel) picking up a high-spirited hitchhiker (Senie Priti), in 2017.

Advertisement

He self-financed it with $35,000 to $40,000 from his savings as a waiter at the Footscray Community Arts Centre cafe and considered it a success when Cerulean Blue premiered at Melbourne International Film Festival in 2019 then was picked up by streaming service Stan. “It didn’t break even because we played festivals and then, when it premiered in late 2019, COVID happened,” he says. “But it developed a name for myself in the industry to be able to get other projects made.” Related Article Cinema Indian films out-perform Australian releases at the local box office Two years ago, Ortega tried Victorian state film agency VicScreen but ended up self-financing his second feature, Westgate, too. It cost $85,000: $70,000 from his savings and the rest from crowdfunding and supporters. “I thought ‘should I put a deposit on a house or should I make a film?’,” he says. “I chose film again.”

Advertisement

Set over 24 hours in 1999, Westgate is a drama about an Italian-Australian single mother (Sarah Nicolazzo) from West Footscray who still carries the trauma from her father being killed in the West Gate Bridge collapse in 1970. It was a personal story for Ortega, 34, who grew up in an Italian/Spanish migrant family in Footscray. “It’s basically my mother’s story,” he says. “Sarah’s basically playing a version of my mother and Julian (Max Nappo) is basically a young version of me.” After premiering at MIFF and screening at SXSW Sydney last year, Westgate had a modest cinema run, was released on DVD and Blu-ray and is now streaming on Prime Video and Apple TV. While it is yet to break even, Ortega thinks it will with more sales over time. He is now planning another feature film but with a difference. “I’d love to not spend my own money on a third one,” he says.

Advertisement

Screen Australia’s latest drama report showed that 34 Australian films, including Westgate, started shooting in 2024-25. While 22 of them cost $1 million-$10 million, three cost less than $1 million. War Machine has been a Netflix hit but only The Travellers ($2 million) and Leviticus ($1.5 million) have made an impact in cinemas so far. That aligns with the findings of Nick Hayes’ recent report Made Not Seen: Australians go to cinemas in large numbers, but Australian film attendance has collapsed to the point where Indian releases are now more successful at the local box office. title: Joyous energy and raucous humour collide in this five-star gig
text:
Advertisement

Key points MUSIC: Belle and Sebastian perform If You’re Feeling Sinister at the Palais

OPERA: Lyric Opera perform a Regency-Era Serse at the Gasworks Theatre

DANCE: 7 Dances for 7 People is performed at Northcote Town Hall

MUSIC

Belle and Sebastian ★★★★★

Palais Theatre, September 12 “Welcome to the second recording session for this still quite-new band,” Stuart Murdoch says with a grin. His tongue is firmly in cheek – Belle and Sebastian, the indie-pop group he’s led for more than half his life, is on tour celebrating its 30th year. In 1996, the bookish Scots made their debut with two albums: Tigermilk and If You’re Feeling Sinister. On this anniversary tour, they’re alternating playing those records in full. Melbourne gets the Sinister treatment. Belle & Sebastian perform at the Palais, September 12, 2026. Richard Clifford Playing albums in full live can be a cynical cash-cow in the age of commodified nostalgia, but there’s no denying the sheer delight of hearing a beloved album like this in all its glory. On record, Sinister’s arrangements are delicate; live, they’re injected with a shot of joyous energy, with buzzing synth to boot. Many of these songs begin with Murdoch alone, singing with that sweet, instantly recognisable voice, before the eight other musicians on stage slowly blossom to create sunlight in musical form. Lead guitarist Stevie Jackson raucously takes on the harmonica for Me and the Major, his movements a chaotic blur.

Advertisement

As the album reaches its halfway point, a projection behind the band shows the LP being flipped on a turntable – “a bit of antiquated attention to detail,” Murdoch says. Eager fans have been dancing in the aisles from the beginning, but when the band plays Get Me Away, I’m Dying, the entire venue is on its feet. The gorgeous Mayfly is another highlight from this half, but really, it’s all joy, not least because Murdoch and co are clearly having a blast, too. Murdoch’s signature humour is on display all night as he intersperses the music with quips, including a spiel about Victoria’s slogans as seen on number plates and a joke about Viagra as he takes his medication on stage. “Back to sweetness and light!” he says, and back they go. Sarah Martin, Stuart Murdoch and Stevie Jackson of Belle & Sebastian. Richard Clifford A guitar-heavy I’m a Cuckoo kicks off the second set, comprising songs from the rest of the band’s long career. Belle and Sebastian have such a varied discography that it’s a grab-bag every night. There are some deeper cuts here, such as 2010’s Little Lou, Ugly Jack, Prophet John, recorded with Norah Jones; here, it’s long-time vocalist Sarah Martin who does the honours, beautiful as ever. 2006’s Funny Little Frog is a charming, nostalgic treat. The band is pulling songs out on the fly by the end, with Another Sunny Day closing the night. It’s apt – with 30 years of sunny days up their sleeves, Belle and Sebastian keep on delivering.

Reviewed by Giselle Au-Nhien Nguyen

Advertisement

OPERA

Serse ★★

Gasworks Theatre, until September 13 We’re all getting restless. Twenty minutes after the curtain was meant to go up for the opening show of Lyric Opera’s Serse, we’re still waiting for the conductor to raise his baton. Eventually, company artistic director and conductor Patrick Burns addresses the audience, explaining that though they’ve tried to fix the issue, they’ve had no success. Baroque opera has a small but loyal audience in Melbourne Jodie Hutchinson Both projectors have died. For the near-three-hour Italian opera we’re about to witness, there will be no surtitles. No translations. Oh dear. Turns out, if it was sung in English, it’d be hard to follow anyway. Handel’s 1738 opera about the King of Persia is one of those operas stacked with couples pursuing, deceiving, rejecting and reuniting with one another, plus disguises and mistaken identities thrown in, of course.

Advertisement

Baroque opera has a small but loyal audience in Melbourne, but for a company that has commendably programmed contemporary operas in previous seasons, Serse is, frankly, an odd choice. The production, by director Beng Oh and designer Christina Logan-Bell, is certainly clever, updated to the Regency era where it fits quite well, what with all the letter-writing and love-in-turmoil. But even with tech issues aside, faults remain. The ornamentation demands were too much for some, and the approach (though it is correct Baroque style) of leaving out vibrato resulted in some unenergised vocal patches. The production, by director Beng Oh and designer Christina Logan-Bell, is certainly clever. Jodie Hutchinson Some shined, like mezzo Naomi Flatman, who with a honeyed, resonant sound, delivered the standout performance of the night. Soprano Rebecca Rashleigh too gave a consistently vibrant performance, with thrilling top notes. As Serse, it was testament to Sally-Anne Russell’s comedic talent that though we mostly had no idea what was going on, people still laughed when they were, presumably, meant to. Though it was the initial problem, the ensuing convoluted plot, repetitive musical style and uneven singing proved that being sung in a foreign language is not the greatest measure of an opera’s accessibility.

Reviewed by Bridget Davies

Advertisement

DANCE

7 Dances for 7 People ★★★

Northcote Town Hall, until September 19 Yes, there are indeed seven dances – or sections – in choreographer Trá Mi Dinh’s latest work, but only the first of them is unambiguously successful. I would happily have watched this strange, lustrous gambit for the full hour, either extended or simply repeated. Tra Mi Dinh and Rachel Coulson in 7 Dances for 7 People. Darren Gill Two dancers emerge from billowing clouds of smoke, like figures in a dream, amid an eerie tintinnabulation. Delicate unison stepping gives their progress toward the audience an insect-like grace; raised arms and joined hands further heighten their otherworldly appearance. The awkward position of the arms, which restricts the movement of the upper body, creates a sense of fragility and risk. It’s as if their grip on one another is all that prevents them tumbling back in the cloud of smoke. It gives the whole scene a shimmery, slippery sort of ephemerality.

Advertisement

After the first dance, the movement becomes more eclectic. Smooth isolations, with their tensing and releasing, give way to looser spinning figures. Vaguely balletic poses contrast with thrusting modern dance gestures. And everything whirls together in the smoke. The combinations are not always compelling, but something of the mysterious atmosphere of the first section persists. And interesting details register throughout, particularly in the way the seven dancers move between pairs and trios, with new arrangement materialising in the gloom. The balletic poses contrast with modern dance gestures as everything whirls together amid the smoke. Darren Gill This show is based on a shorter commission for Lucy Guerin’s Pieces in 2024, and it retains the same production team, including lighting designer Rachel Rui Qian Lee and costume designer Geoffrey Watson, who provides beautiful filmy smocks. Tilman Robinson’s score feels a little too insistent. The opening section with its bells has an attractive alienness, but I think the heavier beats used thereafter impose too much on the choreography and a more ambient soundscape might have been more effective.

Advertisement

Editor's pick Updated

Arts Macy Gray concert at Arts Centre cancelled as staff prepare to strike The work is apparently based on the significance of the number seven across religions and cultural traditions. Yet it is strongest when there is no theme: just fleeting relations between bodies – repetitions and doublings, divergences and singularities – in a world before number settles into meaning.

title: You’ve been put on a performance management plan. Are you on the way out?
text:
Advertisement

BusinessWorkplaceWorkplace You’ve been put on a performance management plan. Are you on the way out? Millie Muroi September 13, 2026 — 10:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When roadside patrol mechanic Yep Yap was sacked in 2022, he’d been put on a performance management plan and failed to meet three key performance indicators. But the Fair Work Commission found the targets set for Yap were unrealistic, unachievable and improper, ultimately forcing his employer, the company Club Assist, to reinstate him with back pay under unfair dismissal laws. Performance management plans are increasingly being used as a tick-the-box exercise towards getting rid of people. Stephen Kiprillis Performance management plans, also known as performance improvement plans (PIPs), have become common as a tool towards dismissing an employee. While meant as a genuine way to improve workers’ performance, they are increasingly being used as a tick-the-box exercise towards getting rid of people and still complying with unfair dismissal laws. In fact, these laws – introduced more than 40 years ago to protect workers from arbitrary, unfair sackings – are what have made PIPs so popular in Australia, says Joydeep Hor of employment law firm People + Culture Strategies.

Advertisement

“There’s no hard and fast rule that says you have to have someone on a PIP before you can terminate their employment for performance reasons, but in the absence of one, there can be some questions asked,” Hor says. Related Article Unfair dismissal Minor change to title costs worker her job So, what should you do if you find yourself on a PIP? How do they work? And what do managers need to know? How does a performance management plan work? When publicist Vivian (who did not use her real name because of concern about future employment prospects) was put on a performance management plan at a public relations agency in Sydney this year, it came as a surprise.

Advertisement

She was told not to mention it to colleagues, was given the option to negotiate a settlement instead and was told she had 24 hours to make her decision. The latter, she found out from a lawyer, was not a time frame the firm could hold her to. Vivian had discussions with the firm’s HR department, her employment lawyer and her manager, and agreed on a set of key performance indicators. For the next few months, her performance was closely monitored. Hor says PIPs are intended as a way to hold both employees and managers to account. “The idea is that an employer should be actively working with a so-called ‘underperforming employee’ to help them improve their performance, using a plan which has metrics and timeframes,” he says. However, the process is often treated as more of a set-and-forget process by managers, who Hor says should be setting expectations early and bringing up concerns informally first.

Advertisement

Does it mean you’re about to get sacked? Vivian says getting put on a performance management plan initially felt like she was getting booted. “The process felt micro-manager-y with regular reviews, but the KPIs weren’t hard to turn around, and I ended up passing it,” she says. “It was a bit awkward afterwards, but that didn’t last too long.” TLB Law & Co senior associate Ellie Wolfenden says PIPs have, in some instances, become a tick-the-box exercise rather than a genuine effort to improve employee performance. “It goes towards an employer demonstrating that the employee knew their performance wasn’t meeting the required standard, knew what the required standards were, and had been offered a fair opportunity to improve their performance,” she says.

Advertisement

Wolfenden says that in some situations, employers set benchmarks that are unreasonable or unrealistic. “That’s when employees can feel that the process is not genuinely aimed at improving their performance, but rather is setting them up to fail,” she says. That can be stressful and troubling, but may also create a work health and safety risk the employer needs to manage, she says. What should you do if you’re put on a PIP? Hor says the first step is generally for employees to clarify why it is happening and exactly what is expected. “If there’s anything ambiguous in terms of a target or a deadline, those things should be clarified in a conversation,” he says.

Advertisement

For employees who have been put on a PIP that feels unreasonable, Wolfenden says it can be worth seeking legal advice, clearly documenting why and how any given metrics may be unreasonable, and to weigh in on what they think is achievable. “We’ve seen some performance management plans where sales tasks and targets are wholly out of proportion to the market and an employee is getting held to KPIs that no one in the business is meeting because of external market factors,” she says. Related Article Opinion

Careers The secret skill to getting what you actually want at work Tim Duggan Work columnist In Yap’s case, the employer’s decision to sack him was overruled because the performance metrics – including needing to aim for a particular rate of battery replacements under warranty – were seen as improper, and because many of the firm’s other roadside patrol officers had failed to meet their KPIs without being sacked. Wolfenden says employees on PIPs should document when they are getting positive reviews or feedback from their broader team and external stakeholders, as well as circumstances outside their control that may impact their performance against requirements of the PIP.

Advertisement

Hor says employees who feel they are being managed out should have honest conversations with their managers. “If the employer is just going through the motions, that’s not very nice, and they shouldn’t be, but there may be opportunities to part ways on an agreed basis and short-circuit what could otherwise be a very unpleasant process for all involved,” he says. Negotiating a mutual separation agreement can also be beneficial for the employer in that they can potentially avoid the time and resources involved in managing a PIP process. “PIPs, when done properly, involve weekly check-ins and providing training and support to the employee to help them improve performance,” Wolfenden says. “It’s not meant to be a hands-off process.” What do employers need to know about PIPs? Hor says employers need to ensure the targets they set are clear, measurable and time-bound, with clearly outlined consequences.

Advertisement

Where a metric is subjective, he says the employer should provide details as to how that subjectivity will be assessed. Wolfenden says while there are guidelines available from the Fair Work Ombudsman and theories of best practice from Fair Work Commission decisions and HR professionals, there are no clear regulations around conducting a PIP. Employers need to make sure PIPs are implemented in a reasonable manner, rather than setting workers up to fail. iStock However, employers need to make sure PIPs are implemented in a lawful and reasonable manner, taking into account general work health and safety principles, and the health circumstances of the employee in question, she says: “There is no one-size-fits-all approach.” Wolfenden says it is also important for employers to consider and account for factual matters outside an employee’s control, which may be affecting their performance.

Advertisement

Ultimately, she says performance management plans should be tailored to genuinely help employees improve. Related Article Opinion

Pay My manager wanted me to argue for a pay rise. Why should I? Jonathan Rivett Careers contributor “Using performance management or improvement plans with the aim of exiting the employee from the business, irrespective of performance improvement by the employee, undermines the purpose of such plans and can open the employer up to a claim,” she says. Australian HR Institute chief executive Sarah McCann-Bartlett says employers also need clear documentation and processes around PIPs. “It is now expected that all discussions are documented by the manager as evidence of these conversations and the supports for the employee to improve their performance having been put in place,” she says.

Advertisement

title: 'It could take over the entire internet': The threat top tech leaders say could arise in a year
text:
in brief Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called on tech firms to slow down frontier AI development.

Rivals Sam Altman and Elon Musk backed the proposal amid growing AI safety concerns.

The boss of one of the world's major artificial intelligence companies has called for an urgent slowdown in development amid mounting fears over the risks of "superintelligent" computer systems and its threat to humanity.

The intervention came after a former employee at Anthropic, which is behind the Claude AI chatbot, warned that AI could kill off humanity in a few years' time.

The company's chief executive Dario Amodei on Sunday (AEST) said he was concerned by AI's ability to self-improve could outrun humanity's ability to control it, and by a recent incident in which rogue AI agents attacked targets they were not asked to.

He offered three-step plan intended to pace development and create more time to manage its risks.

In a lengthy essay shared on X he said: "We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models. Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain".

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"Not building the technology deprives humanity of benefits or simply places AI in the hands of authoritarian powers, while building it too fast is reckless," he added. "We have sought a middle way."

"But over the last few months, I have become convinced that fully addressing the risks requires even more prudence."

His company's competitors agreed. Both Elon Musk, who runs xAI, and Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, quickly chimed in on the social media platform to express agreement with Amodei's assessment.

"Dario is right," Musk wrote, while Altman posted: "Committing to having independent evaluators with employee-like access is a great idea, and we will do the same," adding that more information would be shared soon.

Rogue agents and security risks

Amodei made his essay public after San Francisco-based Anthropic released a threat intelligence report on Thursday detailing how several actors had used its Claude AI models for activities ranging from weapons development and cyber operations to surveillance and fraud.

Amodei pointed to AI's growing ability to improve itself, highlighting long-held concerns about it outpacing human ability to control its operation, along with the recent incident involving OpenAI and Hugging Face as his primary reasons to put the brakes on model advances.

Alarm about the potential harm from AI grew this week when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned, accusing both US tech giants of "gambling with our lives" in the race toward superintelligence.

READ MORE AI escaped its testing sandbox and hacked a website. The law is still catching up

Coxon, 27, who previously worked at OpenAI before joining Anthropic, stated that "the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade".

Anthropic has positioned itself as the more safety-conscious frontier lab, but is not immune to these concerns.

Last week it disclosed another instance of an AI model hacking external systems, after a July incident in which some of its Claude models had hacked into the systems of three companies during cybersecurity tests.

The Reuters news agency reported last week that a swarm of rogue OpenAI agents hijacked a German website and transformed it into a bulletin board for other AI agents.

The plan to slow AI's uncontrolled growth

Amodei cautioned that the Hugging Face breach should not be dismissed as a one-off.

"A swarm of agents essentially acted as a fanatically devoted collective, conducting cybersecurity attacks on targets they were not asked to attack," he explained.

"Given the accelerating rate of AI capability development, it's my worry that in 6-12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet, potentially causing hundreds of billions of dollars in damage."

As part of his proposed framework, Amodei called for embedded independent evaluators with employee-like access to verify safety practices, coordination among frontier AI firms to set safety standards, and international cooperation to manage AI risks.

He noted that a coordinated approach would enable leading US AI companies to carry out necessary safety research without putting themselves at a competitive disadvantage, likely requiring targeted antitrust exemptions in the United States.

However, Amodei emphasized that any slowdown by democratically governed countries should be limited to preserving the lead US AI firms hold over China.

"Pacing within democracies will be limited by the lead that US companies have over authoritarian regimes, chiefly the Chinese Communist Party," Amodei wrote, calling for tighter controls on advanced AI chips, model distillation, and theft of model weights.

There is also an enormous amount of money riding on staying ahead, as both OpenAI and Anthropic prepare for blockbuster initial public offerings.

Still, Amodei insisted he is not calling for halting technical progress altogether, but ensuring companies take adequate time to align and safeguard their models before deployment.

title: 'Their kids have never seen their arm': The tattoos people are desperate to remove
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

For years, getting a tattoo meant accepting it was there to stay.

But when Mike Anderson decided he no longer wanted his ink, he discovered just how difficult it was to undo the permanence.

Unable to find a laser tattoo-removal clinic in Sydney's inner-west, he and his wife decided to open one themselves.

"We grew out of it pretty quickly," Anderson tells SBS News.

Twelve years later, what began as a personal solution has grown into a business spanning 12 locations across NSW, Queensland and the United States — part of a booming industry built around a simple idea: what goes on the skin doesn't necessarily have to stay there.

We are trending heavily towards women. Year on year, it's growing exponentially.

With more than a decade in the industry, Anderson says he has seen his fair share of tattoo regret stories.

"There was one from Bondi that said 'chicken' when they thought it said 'prosper'."

Mike Anderson says getting a tattoo removed can have a meaningful impact on people, especially when the tattoos no longer reflect who they are. Source: SBS News / Jasmine Kassis

Anderson says the rise of fine-line and highly detailed tattoos has brought a new group of clients into removal clinics.

"With more detail comes more opportunity for mistakes and bad work. When they go wrong, they usually go noticeably wrong."

The growing demand for a second chance at unwanted ink is fuelling a booming global industry. The tattoo-removal market was worth an estimated US$1.29 billion ($1.79 billion) in 2025 and is forecast to reach US$4.87 billion ($6.75 billion) by 2034, according to Fortune Business Insights.

Erasing hate

For some clients, the tattoos they want removed carry a darker history — racist symbols, hate-related words and, in some cases, racist slogans.

For five years, Anderson's clinic has run a charity program offering free removal of these tattoos.

"We've done al-Qaeda tattoos, we've done swastikas and white power symbols," he says.

Anderson says the aim is to help clients distance themselves from the beliefs these tattoos represent.

Mike Anderson says many people who visit their clinics for tattoo removal want to distance themselves from the beliefs some of the tattoos represent. Source: SBS News / Jasmine Kassis

"The idea is that we take those tattoos and break the chain of influence, like, nephews, sons [and] daughters are less likely to fall into those same paths."

Anderson says the program attracts a high volume of applicants, but clients must demonstrate genuine remorse.

"We judge it on a case-by-case basis. We ask questions about the crimes they've committed; we expect transparency.

We get a lot of people referred by parole officers, particularly young people who've been under some bad circumstances.

"They have to tell us what it means to them; are they looking to get employed? And make sure they're the right person."

How tattoos went mainstream

Today's tattoo removal industry is part of a much longer story: how tattooing evolved from a practice associated with particular communities and subcultures into mainstream body art.

In Australia, the history stretches back to the convict era.

The State Library of Victoria estimates around a quarter of convicts sent to Australia had at least one tattoo.

Tattoo historian Rhys Gordon says tattooing was pushed into the mainstream between the 1980s and 2000s, taking it beyond its traditional subcultures. Source: SBS News / Jesmine Cheong

Research by historian Simon Barnard, based on more than 10,000 convict records from Van Diemen's Land (modern-day Tasmania), found about 37 per cent of male convicts and 15 per cent of female convicts arrived in the 19th century with tattoos.

He found these tattoos were rarely random; they were carefully chosen and often deeply symbolic.

Tattoo historian and artist Rhys Gordon says some tattooing also took place during the long voyages to Australia aboard convict ships.

"There's evidence of hand-poked tattooing being done on the [convict] ships, and that was maybe the name of a town, a loved one," he tells SBS News.

Many also picked up the art form from settlers seeking fortune during the Gold Rush in the 1850s.

READ MORE The reason an Australian bar company is changing its rules on face tattoos

While tattooing has a long history across many cultures, its history in Australia also intersects with First Nations forms of body modification. Historical accounts distinguish tattooing from practices such as scarification and ceremonial body painting among Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples.

As Sydney and Melbourne grew into major port cities, merchants and other travellers brought European tattooing traditions. Gradually, commercial tattooing developed in Australia, with sailors among its early clientele.

By the 20th century, tattoos were associated with different groups and identities.

"In the 70s, it became the biker culture, rock'n'roll, AC/DC, Rose Tattoo ... this started to have an impact on the youth of the day, and then it sort of spread from there , " Gordon says.

Mike Anderson says for some people, the tattoos they want removed carry a darker history: racist symbols, slogans or hate-related words. Source: NurPhoto / Getty Images

But he says later decades helped push tattooing beyond its traditional subcultures and into the mainstream.

"Now they've set the playing [field] for the newer artists to be able to take it to the next level."

According to 2023 McCrindle research, three in 10 Australians (30 per cent) had a tattoo, compared with 20 per cent in 2018.

A cultural archive

Hong Kong-style tattoo artist Jonathan Tsang has built a global following by taking his work on the road, setting up temporary studios in cities around the world.

He's currently in Melbourne until mid-September, attracting clients from across Australia and beyond.

For tattoo artist Jonathan Tsang, tattoos are more than designs — they can act as a cultural archive or preserve a connection. Source: SBS News / Jasmine Kassis

Tsang believes the bold dragon, tiger, and eagle designs once strongly associated with sailors, gangs and other subcultures live on as a form of cultural expression.

"Back in the day, it was seen only on sailors or gangs in Hong Kong, but nowadays it's more of an appreciation for the style," he tells SBS News.

Tsang says tattoos are more than designs: they can act as a cultural archive, preserving a connection to a moment, a history and place in time. He says, just like sailors, migrants often choose ink to represent their journeys.

"Sometimes immigrants that live in Australia see it as an identity thing."

Ink as identity

Gordon, who has been tattooing for 36 years and specialises in Japanese-style tattooing at his parlour in Queensland's Surfers Paradise, says demand for cultural and identity-driven tattoos is strong as ever.

"So many sub-cultures and sub-sections have embraced tattooing; anime tattooing is probably one of the biggest movements. It appeals to anyone and everyone," he says.

"Here in Australia now it's great to see Samoa[ns], Māori, Polynesians from all aspects embracing their culture and getting covered.

It's beautiful, power[ful] and there is so much connection to the land and history.

But cultural tattooing is not limited to people of that particular heritage, Gordon says, pointing to his own tattoos as an example.

"I've never had an adverse reaction by a Japanese person [to] me wearing Japanese culturally significant tattoos," he says.

"If anything, they're like, 'Man, this is amazing; good for you'.

"It's freedom of expression and society is now accepting people's choices in life."

Tattoo historian and artist Rhys Gordon specialises in Japanese-style tattooing at his parlour in Queensland's Surfers Paradise. Source: SBS News / Jesmine Cheong

For Anderson, that freedom can also mean having the choice to let go of something once considered permanent.

Reflecting on the clients who have come through his charity program seeking to remove hate symbols, he says the impact can extend well beyond the tattoo itself.

"We've had clients in tears. Their kids have never seen their arm; they've never worn shorts to the beach.

It can have a really meaningful impact.

title: Australians love traveling to the UK. They could soon be paying more
text:
In brief Regional cities in the UK will be able to start charging a tourist levy later this year.

The proposal will bring British cities in line with many other international destinations.

The bill is about to get steeper for the 1.2 million Australians who travel to the UK every year as British mayors will soon have the power to charge a so-called "tourist tax" on accommodation.

Last week the UK government announced it was going to be pressing ahead with the controversial levy which Prime Minister Andy Burnham — the so called "King of the North" — hopes will help move power and money way from London.

Called the "Overnight Visitor Levy," it gives regional mayors the option to tax people on a percentage of their stays at hotels, bed and breakfasts and other types of accommodation.

Burnham— who replaced Keir Starmer as prime minister in July— sees the levy as a way of financially empowering regional cities.

He said last week the tax would come into force towards the end of the next financial year, with mayors expected to set out spending plans for the funds raised by early 2028.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

But the plan has parts of the UK economy worried.

What does it mean for tourists?

The levy will be set at the discretion of city councils but on Friday Labour mayors in 10 regional cities said they would cap the charge the charge at five per cent, following widespread concerns from the hospitality industry that the levy would dampen spending.

An exact date for the levy's introduction has not been announced but Burnham said the tax would come into force towards the end of next financial year and apply to both Britons and international tourists.

The exact terms of the levy could vary from city to city, but mayors in London, Greater Manchester, Liverpool City Region, West Midlands, North East, West of England, West Yorkshire, South Yorkshire, East Midlands and York and North Yorkshire have all agreed to the five per cent cap.

Two Reform UK mayors and two Conservative party mayors have said they would oppose any levy — so its possible the price of accommodation will go up in some cities, but not others.

Is this a new idea?

While the five per cent levy would be new for regional cities in Britain, it's not a UK first.

In July, Edinburgh launched a 5 per cent levy on accommodation that's capped at five nights and similar taxes are already common around the world.

New York, LA, Brussels, Amsterdam, Toronto and Montreal all have their own equivalent charges.

Wales is set to introduce it's own £1.30 per person per night levy in April of next year.

How has it been received in the UK?

The move has not been supported by UKHospitality, which represents the sector. It said the move would hurt British families and add to red tape.

"Give mayors one tax-raising power on one sector and they will pull that lever until it snaps," said Chief Executive Allen Simpson.

Simpson cited research by consultancy Oxford Economics estimating that a fully implemented 5% levy by 2030 would cost around 33,000 jobs and reduce economic output by £2.2 billion ($2.98 billion).

The industry also argues that British hospitality already pays 20% sales tax, double the norm across much of Europe.

title: Middle East shipping escalation about to hit every Australian wallet
text:
in brief Escalating conflict in the Middle East pushed Australian unleaded petrol prices to $2.11 per litre.

Experts warn high fuel costs will persist and could prompt further central bank rate hikes.

Australians are being warned that high fuel prices are likely to stay as the war in the Middle East reaches dangerous new levels of escalation.

As the US-led war on Iran shows no signs of ending and oil tankers are being targeted and sunk in the Strait of Hormuz by both sides, global oil prices have surged above US $100 ($139.5) a barrel.

This has led to fuel prices in Australia jumping at the bowser to an average price for regular unleaded of $2.11, a massive increase from $1.55 in July.

For diesel, oil prices increased almost 50 per cent since June.

The surging prices are sparking inflation fears and raising concerns that the Reserve Bank of Australia will lift the cash rate when the monetary policy board meets again at the end of September.

High fuel prices were the "new norm", NRMA spokesman Peter Khoury said.

"It really depends exclusively, almost, on what's going to happen in the Middle East," he said.

"We've seen dangerous levels of escalation in the last few days, so you've got the situation where they're blowing up each other's oil tankers in the ocean, so that doesn't help."

In response to soaring prices at the start of the conflict in the Middle East in March, the Albanese government temporarily halved the fuel excise in April, slashing 26 cents off a litre.

A scaled-back extension of the fuel excise was reduced to 16 cents per litre for petrol and diesel, which lasted until 2 August.

Khoury said the government keeping its options open remained the best approach to the unfolding crisis.

Khoury urged motorists to check fuel prices in real-time and shop around for savings when filling up.

title: Fixing Australia's immigration system is not just about cutting migrants
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

After the COVID-19 pandemic, the number of migrants flowing into Australia increased to "unbelievable levels", says immigration expert Abul Rizvi.

Numbers had fallen sharply during the pandemic years as lockdown measures halted international travel. By March 2021, quarterly migrant arrivals had dropped to a fifth of pre-pandemic levels in Australia.

As things returned to normal, that trend reversed.

Rizvi, a former deputy secretary at the Department of Immigration, says no one was expecting net overseas migration (NOM) — which also factors in migrant departures — to reach a record annual high of almost 550,000 people as it did in 2023.

Almost three years later, Australia is still adjusting to that influx, and politicians across the ideological divide are now fixated on setting a new figure.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The recent debate over Australia's NOM has been dominated by One Nation, which is calling for substantial cuts to immigration.

But research shows that opposition to immigration is often concentrated in areas with the fewest migrants.

Experts say these areas could also be among the worst hit by wide-ranging cuts, such as those proposed by One Nation.

Australia's temporary migration challenge

Temporary migrants have historically been a driver of population growth in Australia. Typically, more migrants arrive each year than those who leave, increasing the overall population over time.

One Nation leader Pauline Hanson has accused Labor of using migration to prop up headline economic numbers, saying in a media release: "Australians pay the price through lower wages, higher rents, unaffordable homes and stretched services."

To address these issues, Hanson says the number of migrants should be reduced, insisting that "international student numbers must be slashed". She has also called for the skilled migration program to be more targeted, and immigration from countries on the 'Do Not Travel' list to be halted.

The latest Department of Home Affairs figures show 2.9 million temporary visa holders were living in Australia on 31 July 2026.

New Zealand citizens can access a special temporary visa (subclass 444) that allows them to remain in Australia indefinitely. This has been available for decades but a direct pathway for citizenship was also created in 2023. Source: SBS News

The largest single group was New Zealanders holding 'special category visas', which accounted for 20 per cent (736,509) of temporary visa holders.

Temporary visa holders, who also include tourists or those undertaking short-term work or study, are not considered migrants by the ABS unless they are in the country for longer than a year.

Global migration expert and associate professor at the University of Sydney, Anna Boucher, says some temporary visa holders are still in Australia due to decisions made by former governments, including extensions granted after the pandemic by the Coalition to aid economic recovery and bridge skill shortages.

"These migration legacies can last a long time," Boucher says.

Who is considered a migrant?

To count migrant arrivals, the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) looks at a person's "usual residence", using criteria such as whether they have lived in the country for 12 months or more over the 16-month period after arriving.

The latest ABS overseas migration data shows 568,400 migrants arrived in Australia in financial year 2024/25, and 262,800 left. These figures are used to calculate NOM, which was 305,600.

The ABS also releases NOM figures for calendar years. In 2024, NOM was 340,800, falling to 301,100 in 2025.

This is substantially lower than the peak in 2023, when 547,300 people entered the country, but still slightly higher than yearly figures before the pandemic.

Net overseas migration (NOM) looks at how many longer-term migrants are arriving in Australia each year. Source: SBS News

Data shows migrants on temporary visas made up 70 per cent of NOM in 2024/25.

Net overseas migration includes Australian citizens returning after living overseas for an extended period (although more Australians left in 2024/25 than returned), as well as New Zealanders, and those on temporary and permanent visas. Source: SBS News

Who are Australia's temporary migrants?

Bringing down the number of temporary migrants would involve reducing the number of temporary visas issued each year.

Hanson has said she would target international students and temporary graduate visa holders in an effort to cut NOM to 130,000. In 2024/25, students made up 43 per cent of temporary migrant arrivals.

Temporary migrants make up a large percentage of net overseas migration numbers. They include students, skilled workers and backpackers as well as 'visitors' who originally entered Australia on a tourist or other short-term visa, but extended their stay, often for work or study purposes. Source: SBS News

But Rizvi says a massive cut to student visas would have adverse effects on universities and could jeopardise the jobs of 50,000 Australians working in the international education sector.

He points out almost half of Sydney University's revenue comes from tuition fees paid by international students.

The consequences would be severe and I don't think [Hanson] has thought about those consequences.

Rizvi says it's easier to make small cuts to many visa categories than to make big cuts to one or two, as the "negative consequences become quite extreme".

But One Nation's ambitious target to bring NOM down to 130,000 would require a dramatic cut of 175,700 people per year, based on 2024/25 figures.

This could not be achieved even if all 156,700 temporary migrants on student visas each year were cut.

Labor is aiming for a more modest reduction, bringing NOM down to 225,000 within two years, according to its budget projections for 2027/28.

The Coalition says it expects NOM to be "substantially below 200,000" under its policy to cap numbers based on housing supply.

Will cuts make life better?

One reason often cited for cutting immigration is to improve housing affordability.

Boucher says reducing immigration could potentially improve rental affordability, but the impact would mostly be felt in parts of the major capital cities, particularly if cuts target international students.

Almost all students on a temporary visa live in a capital city (around 90 per cent), according to the latest Census data from 2021.

Even in the major cities, the impact on housing demand would likely be marginal, Rizvi says.

[For] people in Sydney, it would make a minimal difference in terms of their financial situation.

Boucher points out that property prices are driven by a range of factors, including the tax system and interest rate rises. Additionally, because migrant labour contributes to the construction of housing, cutting NOM could have other unintended consequences for the housing market, making the overall impact "hard to predict".

Other potential benefits, such as reduced traffic congestion, are also unlikely to be very noticeable, says Rizvi.

Four out of five temporary residents lived in a capital city, and around half lived in Sydney and Melbourne, according to the 2021 Census. Source: SBS News

On the flip side, the negative impacts of reducing NOM could include driving up prices for delivery services and food, and disruption to healthcare services.

Grattan Institute analysis of 2016 Census data found the hospitality industry had the largest share of migrant workers, with 40 per cent born overseas. Migrants made up almost half of all chefs and cooks in Australia.

It also found the healthcare and social assistance sector relies heavily on migrants, with around 37 per cent of these workers born overseas. Permanent migrants made up around one quarter of all registered nurses in the sector. They also work as aged and disabled carers, child carers and nursing support staff.

What about regional and rural areas?

Grattan's analysis found that mining areas, such as the Pilbara in remote Western Australia, are more likely to rely on migrant workers, and some agricultural areas have higher shares of working holiday makers. The sunny climate of the Gold Coast is attractive to many New Zealanders.

According to the 2021 Census, around 20 per cent of working holiday makers in Australia live in regional or rural Queensland.

Hanson, who hails from Queensland and is a senator for the state, has acknowledged the importance of seasonal workers to rural and regional communities. More specifically, she's said she wants to maintain the number of workers brought in from Pacific countries and Timor-Leste through the PALM scheme (around 30,000 workers in March 2024), even though this would likely raise NOM above One Nation's target.

But she insists this won't impact the cost of housing in rural and regional areas because these workers are often given accommodation by their employers.

"Rural and regional Australia would die if they didn't have the workers coming in, especially the abattoirs and farmers, so that's a different program," Hanson told reporters at News Corp's Bush Summit last month.

One Nation leader Pauline Hanson (centre) and Nationals Leader Matt Canavan (right) at the Bush Summit in Dubbo on 27 August. Source: AAP / Pip Farquharson

One Nation and the Nationals have both criticised the Albanese government's decision to slow down the processing of working holiday visas, saying backpackers were not taking houses from people in Sydney, Melbourne or Brisbane.

But a 2021 report by Grattan, titled "Rethinking permanent skilled migration after the pandemic", noted anti-migrant views appear to be more prevalent in regional Australia, even though there are far fewer migrants there, especially from parts of Asia, the Middle East and Africa.

"This suggests a sense of threat can be as important as the level of threat," the report said.

What is the problem that needs fixing?

While simply cutting migration may not solve Australia's cost of living issues, past analysis has suggested more nuanced changes to the system could help ensure it benefits the country.

The Parkinson review of the migration system in 2023 criticised Australia's reliance on temporary migrants.

"It is not in Australia's national interest to maintain a large proportion of temporary entrants with no pathway to citizenship as it undermines our democratic resilience and social cohesion," the report said.

Experts at the Grattan Institute say it's important to get Australia's temporary intake right because most permanent visas are granted to temporary residents already in Australia.

Its report suggested allowing all migrants earning wages above a certain level to be eligible for a temporary visa, rather than restricting this to certain occupations. This would address most skills shortages, simplify sponsorship pathways for employers and limit exploitation of lower-paid workers.

It would also boost the pool of high-quality applicants for permanent residency.

Visas that offer a pathway to permanent residency should be restricted to younger workers under the age of 30, the report suggests.

It also cautioned the government against increasing the number of migrants filling low-skilled jobs in Australia, as they could "undercut the wages of low-paid Australians and further increase exploitation".

In their essay On Our Terms, former immigration policy adviser Henry Sherrell and tax researcher Lachlan Vass suggest the goal of immigration policy should be to make the lives of Australians better.

The visa system should pick people deliberately, across all parts of the system, to benefit Australians.

They say Australia needs an explicit target for migration as this would provide a clear long-term signal to state governments, employers and citizens.

The authors recommended setting net migration at 1 per cent of population growth.

"Beyond which the costs grow quickly and political support wilts [according to historical observations]," the authors note.

Australian migration is currently above 1 per cent, but the government is forecasting a rate of about 0.9 per cent in 2026/27, falling to 0.8 in 2027/28, which the authors believe is "about right".

The difficulty is getting to this figure.

Careful changes required to avoid unintended consequences

While Labor, the Coalition and One Nation have all promised to bring down NOM, no one has yet set out how this will be done, a sign of how challenging it is to balance competing interests.

"Any time you make a cut, you're going to have to upset [a particular] group," Boucher says.

Businesses want to retain skilled migrants as well as working holidaymakers who are often employed on farms; migrants want visas for family members; and those living in tourist areas also want to retain backpackers. Migrants also make a significant contribution in funding Australia's higher education sector.

Reducing immigration will impact Australia's economy because it reduces tax and visa revenue and slows population growth, which can lead to lower household consumption and reduced business profits.

A Treasury paper published in 2021 estimates that each skilled migrant provides a $198,000 benefit to the Australian economy because they generally arrive in the country after finishing their education. The average Australian costs the budget $85,000 across their lifetime because they receive more money back in services than they pay in taxes.

Skilled migrants often contribute more in taxes than they receive in services, and certain sectors such as healthcare rely heavily on overseas workers. Source: Getty / Nansan Houn

Boucher points to the UK, which is facing skills shortages in sectors like construction, healthcare, hospitality and skilled trades, after its work visas were tightened.

She says it's important Australia understands how to fill gaps if it cuts the supply of certain workers, and to be realistic about how quickly domestic workers can be trained to take their place.

A crackdown on bridging visas, which allow migrants to stay in Australia while their immigration status is being resolved, may also involve limiting or rescinding people's current legal appeal rights.

"[Cutting immigration could also] have impacts on things like human rights, like the right to reunify with family."

Where can we cut?

Although they don't agree with slashing international student numbers as Hanson has suggested, both Rizvi and Boucher believe student visas could be tightened — which Labor already appears to be doing.

One area of reform could be the 485 visa, which allows international students to live, study and work in Australia after completing their studies.

Sherrell and Vass have also suggested limiting temporary visas to a maximum of eight years, which would provide a firm deadline for people to transition to a permanent visa, or leave Australia.

Incentives could also be introduced to encourage people to leave Australia voluntarily when their visas expire. This could include allowing overstayers — those currently subject to re-entry bans — to make further visa applications from outside the country.

Superannuation taxes could also be waived, and a cash incentive of $20,000 to $30,000 paid when someone returns to their country of origin.

"This funding is comparatively cheap compared to endless weeks spent in immigration detention. And it is more compassionate too," Sherrell and Vass note.

READ MORE Cost of Nauru deportation deal revealed in late-night inquiry as PM pressed on lack of detail

Senator Jonathon Duniam, the Coalition's spokesperson for home affairs, told ABC's Insiders on 6 September that the government should find a way to deport the 77,000 illegal overstayers in Australia, and suggested temporary visa holders should be required to apply for further visas offshore.

Duniam pointed to the UK's introduction of a 'safe countries of origin' list that designates countries as generally having no serious risk of persecution and allowing for fast-track deportations.

One Nation has gone further, suggesting Australia not accept refugees from countries that the government deems unsafe for Australians to visit, citing Nepal as an example following the country’s recent devastating floods.

But cracking down on Australia's relatively low refugee intake is unlikely to shift migration numbers significantly.

READ MORE The long wait for permanency in Australia's shrinking humanitarian program

One Nation hasn't clarified whether it would reduce current humanitarian numbers from 20,000, which Prime Minister Anthony Albanese recently confirmed the government would maintain.

This is lower than Labor's previously stated target of 27,000 by 2025, but higher than the 13,750 the party was reportedly recently considering cutting it to.

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor hasn't specified a number for the Coalition's refugee intake but says it will be below the former Morrison government's level of 17,875.

Boucher points out that targeting one specific group or visa class as a means of controlling migration has its limits.

If you cut [visas] in one area, how do you now that family migration is not going to spike?

She says prospective applicants will adapt to policy changes and look for workarounds; for example, a cut to student visas could trigger a spike in partner visas.

"It's in the fine grain that the decisions have to be made and that's what makes it such a challenging policy area."

title: Another major bank tips interest rates will rise before year’s end

Westpac's economists finally joined their big bank peers this week, predicting the Reserve Bank of Australia is now likely to lift interest rates this year, instead of staying on hold.

title: Could Australia's housing downturn push the economy into recession?
text:
IN BRIEF Economists say a 10% house price fall could weigh on spending, but would be unlikely to cause a recession alone.

Retail spending and the jobs market could show whether Australia's housing slump is spreading through the economy.

Australians have watched the value of their homes soar for years. Now, as prices head in the opposite direction, there are warnings the fallout could spread well beyond the property market.

Property developer Nigel Satterley has warned Australia could face a "full-blown recession" if the housing downturn spills into consumer spending, as falling property values leave households feeling poorer and less willing to spend.

The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) has pushed back on those fears, acknowledging the downturn will slow parts of the economy but saying it does not currently expect a recession.

Which poses the question: How worried should Australians be?

Independent economist Saul Eslake agrees with the RBA that the housing downturn is likely to slow economic growth, but says falling property prices alone are unlikely to be enough to push Australia into recession.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"I don't think a decline in property prices of the orders of magnitude that people are now talking about ... that is to say, maybe of the order of 10, perhaps in some cities 15 per cent over a one or two-year period, I don't think that on its own would precipitate a recession," he said.

"It would certainly contribute at the margin to some slowing in economic growth."

AMP Chief Economist Shane Oliver also believes a recession is not the most likely outcome, but sees a greater risk that the housing downturn could contribute to one if prices continue falling and the broader economy weakens.

"Recession isn't my base case, but the risk is significant," he said, putting the probability at around 30 per cent and rising.

Why falling house prices can affect how we spend

At the heart of the concern is something economists call the "wealth effect".

Put simply, when the value of an asset such as a home rises, people can feel wealthier and become more comfortable spending. When its value falls, the opposite can happen.

Oliver said previous RBA analysis suggested a 10 per cent fall in house prices could reduce consumer spending by about 0.8 per cent after six months and 1.6 per cent over the longer term.

That matters because household consumption makes up a significant portion of economic activity.

"If the economy is weak enough to start with because of higher interest rates and other things, then that could potentially knock us into recession because the consumer is about 60 per cent of the economy," Oliver said.

But Eslake said the relationship between property values and spending was not necessarily straightforward.

For most Australians who own only the home they live in, he said its value was largely "paper wealth" unless they sold.

If someone is selling to buy another property, falling prices also mean the home they are moving into is likely to be cheaper.

"So they're not necessarily worse off in a real or tangible sense," he said.

Earlier this week, RBA assistant governor Sarah Hunter also said the impact of falling house prices on consumer spending was likely to be relatively small.

What about Australians who recently bought?

Both economists pointed to negative equity as a potentially greater concern for some recent home buyers.

Negative equity occurs when the amount someone owes on their mortgage exceeds the value of their property.

Eslake said that position only becomes a tangible loss if someone is forced to sell, for example, because of unemployment, relocation or a relationship breakdown.

Independent economist Saul Eslake says the relationship between property values and spending is not necessarily straightforward. Source: AAP / Andrew Matthews /PA /Alamy

But simply knowing they are in negative equity could also cause households to cut spending and pay down their mortgage faster.

Oliver said recent buyers were likely to be particularly sensitive to falling prices.

"If you paid $1 million a year ago [and] it's now worth $800,000, you may not feel so happy, particularly ... if your mortgage is worth more than the value of the house," he said.

Could it spiral into something worse?

Oliver told SBS News that retail and consumer spending would probably be among the first places a more serious housing downturn would become visible.

In a worst-case scenario, falling property prices could make households spend less, hurting businesses and employment.

Higher unemployment could then leave more homeowners struggling with mortgages and put further downward pressure on property prices.

"You get this downward spiral, where falling house prices lead to a loss of wealth, leads to less spending, which leads to higher unemployment, which in turn leads to further falls in house prices," Oliver said.

But neither economist believes Australia is there yet.

The latest national accounts show the economy grew 2.1 per cent over the year to the June quarter, while Eslake pointed to continued employment growth and an unemployment rate of around 4.5 per cent.

"I can understand quite a significant proportion of the population will be feeling financial difficulty, pressure or stress," he said.

"That's not the same thing as a recession, and I don't think we are on the brink of one at the moment."

What are the warning signs?

Oliver said Australians should watch whether house price declines accelerate, followed by weakening household spending, fewer job vacancies and eventually rising unemployment.

Eslake similarly nominated employment, job advertisements and business confidence as important indicators.

Both also said a recession would likely require something more than falling house prices alone.

Eslake said another two or three interest rate increases over the next six to nine months would increase the risk, while an external economic or financial shock could also push Australia closer to recession.

READ MORE Home prices fall across Australia as housing downturn takes hold

Oliver said the RBA also had the ability to change course if conditions deteriorated significantly.

"If it looks like a property downturn could drive a recession, they could quickly ... refocus from worried about inflation to worried about recession and higher unemployment," he said.

For now, Eslake believes some of the dire warnings should be treated cautiously.

"I think some of the people in property interests are talking their own book."

title: Regional Australians want cheaper flights. What’s standing in the way?
text:
Bush communities are begging for more budget airfares even as regional airline Rex warns that stiff competition in small markets is pushing the airline to the brink.

Isolated and aging populations are being let down by expensive ticket costs, Madeleine Lawler, chief executive of Regional Development Australia on the Mid North Coast of NSW, warned.

Her comments came during the latest public hearing into the state of Australia's regional aviation sector.

Flights from Coffs Harbour or Port Macquarie cost about 71 cents per kilometre, but from Ballina, where budget flights are available on Jetstar, the average is 12 cents per kilometre, Lawler told the inquiry.

"When I first moved to Coffs Harbour, I was able to get a Bonza flight for under 100 bucks, or Tiger Air was in there for a while, and I was able to get around in a really affordable way," she said.

"We are slicing demand out of our economies by not having those lower price points available in the market, and that means our tourism economies suffer as well."

But half-empty planes could not cover the costs required to run a flight, so Rex shared the burden with travellers from the bush or cancelled services, the struggling airline's network strategy general manager Warrick Lodge told the hearing.

"You end up in a situation where ... carriers are forced to charge each of those passengers more to try and cover their costs," he said.

In July 2024, Rex entered voluntary administration only to be kept afloat with a taxpayer-funded package of $40 million before being bought by American company Air T in December 2025.

Despite this, it was forced to end its Melbourne to Albury route.

Rex had already provided 40,000 seats a year to a market that only had 22,000 passengers — then Qantas added another 31,000.

The airline chose to redirect services to the Melbourne to Devonport service.

Across the business, some Rex routes barely covered operating costs, while others were forced to contribute to overheads, Lodge said.

The airline has deals in place with the Queensland and WA governments, which subsidise operations in those states.

The Royal Flying Doctor Service told the hearing that regional airlines are critical to their operations.

Adequate air travel supported early intervention and helped patients avoid emergency treatment.

"Many of these flights will be to retrieve Australians who are critically ill and need urgent medical evacuation," federation chief executive Emma Buchanan said.

title: A 16-hour flight, 100,000 fans and an upset: The NFL makes its Australian debut
text:
In brief More than 100,000 people attended the NFL's season opener in Melbourne.

Nearly half the crowd was expected to be tourists from interstate and overseas.

More than 100,000 fans from across Australia and abroad flooded the Melbourne Cricket Ground (MCG) on Friday to watch the San Francisco 49ers thrash the Los Angeles Rams 27-7 in the NFL's first-ever regular-season game in Australia.

With the match kicking off at 10am to line up with US prime time, one Rams fan at the MCG described it as the earliest he'd ever been up for a game.

"The atmosphere, I love it, but it's kind of quiet," he told SBS News. "You know, back home it would usually be a bit crazier, with both teams going at it."

"But Melbourne is beautiful, I love it," he added.

Another fan was adding Melbourne to a list of 43 overseas stadiums he'd visited. His white jersey was embroidered with patches representing each country, with a small green patch featuring a cluster of koalas to represent Melbourne on the bottom left.

"I've been to every stadium in the world where the NFL plays," he told SBS News. "It's my first time in Australia, and I love it, everyone is so nice and inviting and helpful."

"I flew all the way in from Miami, Florida, two days ago, and I'm going home tonight. I just came to witness this amazing stadium and the great people of Melbourne."

READ MORE How an NFL match in Melbourne came to be, and its historic links

Friday's game was the first of a four-year deal between Australia and the NFL, but with no guarantee a game will be played here every year, thousands of overseas fans made the pilgrimage.

A sea of red, white, blue and yellow filled the MCG, with a sold-out crowd of 100,022 fans, including thousands of visitors from the US. Almost half of spectators were expected to be from interstate or overseas, according to the state government.

Los Angeles resident Nancy Gakere took advantage of the opportunity for a holiday, stopping over in Fiji on the way to and from Melbourne to break up what could have been a 16-hour direct flight.

She said the journey was more than worth it, especially as the 49ers, pegged as the underdogs, pulled off a surprise rout.

"Everything was just great; honestly, we couldn't have planned it any better," she told SBS News.

"When this away game happened to be in Australia, we thought, why not? And we booked the trip as soon as tickets came out in April, so we have been excited about it for a while."

When Gakere saw that the 49ers away game was set for Melbourne, she saw the opportunity for a holiday down under. Source: Supplied / Nancy Gakere

"And being 49ers fans, we were not the favourites, so we came in with low expectations, and winning was a nice surprise."

Gakere said that staying in Brunswick, in Melbourne's north, had made the trip economical.

"Other than the Uber from the airport, we have just been taking the tram in and out of the city to sight-see, trying food, the bars, walking around and exploring," she told SBS News. "And we went to the Great Ocean Road, which was our main tourism activity."

Gakere said she was a little worried about Melbourne's weather forecast, but game day was a perfect sunny day. Source: Supplied / Nancy Gakere

SBS News spoke with three 49ers fans donning vibrant red jerseys and flat caps in front of the stadium before the match.

"This is amazing," said one.

"We're just so excited; 49ers fans, we're joyous all the time. It's a gathering for us. We do it every year, we just get to do it overseas this year," another fan said.

"Thank you, Melbourne, thank you, thank you. And thank you for the hospitality," another in the trio chimed in. "I was getting on the train this morning, and I was going the wrong way, and this guy pulled me on my jacket and said, 'No, you gotta go that way! The stadium is that way!'"

"Amazing people," the third friend said. "We love the hospitality, food, coffee, oh my gosh, everything has been so amazing. The trip down under has been surreal, thank you guys, we appreciate it."

Consequences of California time for the Rams

In the weeks leading up to the event, popular discussion centred on the two California-based teams' wildly different approaches to navigating the long flight and 17-hour time zone difference to Melbourne.

To the dismay of many Australian commentators, the Rams had jetted in just the morning before, with flights booked straight out after the game.

Whether the decision to keep the Rams on California time affected the team's prowess will be debated. But reigning MVP quarterback Matthew Stafford and star off-season acquisition Myles Garrett were undoubtedly bested by their San Francisco counterparts, who arrived a week earlier to acclimatise.

"Just so proud of this team. Hey, we embraced going to Australia — 15-hour flight, we're here the whole week. It was a grind, but we did it," said 49ers tight end George Kittle.

The Rams entered this new NFL season as the clear favourites to win a Super Bowl being held at their SoFi Stadium home in Los Angeles in February, with a formidable defence bolstered by Garrett.

Los Angeles Rams tight end Colby Parkinson is tackled by San Francisco 49ers cornerback Deommodore Lenoir during the second half of the first NFL match in Melbourne. Source: AAP / Scott Barbour

But the giant crowd packing into the MCG — the seventh-biggest ever for a regular-season NFL game despite an unusual morning kickoff time to accommodate US television audiences — skewed toward San Francisco.

"I love when they [Rams] came out and they were booing. We was out here for a week. We enjoyed the city. I don't think you can fly 16 hours and be ready to play," 49ers receiver Deebo Samuel Jr. told Channel Seven.

title: Card surcharges are ending soon. But the shake-up could come at a cost
text:
In brief From 1 October, credit and debit card purchases will be free from surcharges in Australia.

Banks are expected to respond by raising annual fees and offering fewer perks.

Those irritating and often uneven percentages added to bills when you tap to pay will disappear next month, but the cost of using plastic won’t vanish, and prices are set to rise.

Eftpos, Visa, Mastercard, American Express, JCB, and UnionPay purchases will be free from card surcharges from 1 October, saving consumers an estimated $1.6 billion per year. However, because surcharges cover some merchants' banking costs, prices are expected to rise.

The removal of surcharge fees is one of three changes being rolled out by the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) from next month. Interchange fees, which banks charge when they process domestic card transactions, will be capped at 0.3 per cent on each payment, down from 0.8 per cent.

Merchants typically absorb these costs, and Treasury estimates the changes will save small businesses a combined $910 million a year.
