And because those fees subsidise frequent flyer and rewards points programs, banks have already started raising annual fees and offering fewer perks.

Finder personal finance specialist Taylor Blackburn told SBS news that some deals at Westpac, ANZ, HSBC, MyCard, and BOQ have either changed or are slated to change from 30 September.

Taylor Blackburn, personal finance specialist at Finder, suggests shopping around for a better deal. Source: Supplied / Finder.com

"Sign-up bonus offers have already changed at ANZ, for example, they used to do a $200 credit on your first annual fee, but they're getting rid of that," Blackburn said.

Other frequent flyer bonus offer cards have dropped by 50,000 bonus points, but some banks are improving their offers, so shop around for a better deal now before you get stung by shifting offers, he suggested.

Westpac is lifting interest rates on some of its credit cards and will increase annual fees. NAB credit card interest rates will rise 1.5 per cent too.

Commonwealth Bank announced its Commbank Awards program is changing how consumers earn points in a new loyalty and points scheme.

St George Bank is also lifting interest rates on its Amplify Qantas Platinum credit card and introducing an annual fee of $125. The bank has also dropped the interest-free period on purchases by 10 days.

New interchange caps for foreign-issued cards will start from 1 April 2027.

Australian Banking Association (ABA) chief executive Simon Birmingham said last year that interchange fees in Australia are "already among the lowest in the world".

"We agree with the RBA's concerns about fairness for small businesses, but there are better, more targeted ways to address this without destabilising the broader payments system — such as a small business interchange rate."

The European Union caps fees for debit cards at 0.2 per cent and consumer credit cards at 0.3 per cent.

In the US, rates typically range between 1.15 per cent to 3.3 per cent plus a small flat fee per transaction.

READ MORE How to slash your bills and get money back into your pocket quickly

The third RBA reform starting in October will force EFTPOS, Mastercard and Visa to publish the merchant fees they charge so businesses can compare rates and avoid paying higher-than-average fees.

Birmingham said banks are supporting their business customers to prepare for the changes.

"While the RBA estimates that only one in every six businesses choose to apply a card surcharge, it's a practice that Australians will be happy to see the back of," Birmingham said.

"From next month, the price consumers see in the aisle or on the menu will be the price they pay at the checkout. Similarly, when you shop or pay a bill online, you won't be hit with a card surcharge when you enter your payment details."

COSBOA CEO Skye Cappuccio wants more support for small businesses. Source: Supplied / COSBOA

Council of Small Business Organisations Australia (COSBOA) CEO Skye Cappuccio told SBS News hospitality and tourism businesses with tight margins that also process lots of card transactions will find the extra cost of not surcharging will add up quickly.

"Businesses that feel they have a limited ability to increase prices are highly concerned," said Cappuccio. "We would have preferred to see the interchange fee changes fully rolled out first, so small businesses knew how their payment costs would change before needing to re-cost products and services, update systems and redo business budgets.

"The priority now is making sure they have clear information from providers and that lower payment costs genuinely flow through to the businesses that need them."

title: The hidden $140 billion economy helping some Australians get ahead
text:
Key Points Three in 10 homeowners say they received family help to buy, up from about one in 10 four years ago.

From free childcare to groceries and bills, family support is reshaping what financial independence looks like.

From free childcare to home deposits, groceries and holidays, billions of dollars are flowing between Australian generations long before an inheritance is handed down.

For Shane and Catherine, being grandparents to 10 children can sometimes resemble a full-time job.

A busy week can involve seeing one or more of their grandchildren almost every day, from picking them up from school, taking them to sport, helping with homework and cooking for them.

The couple, who have both worked as educators for 45 years, made a conscious decision to become active grandparents.

Catherine even reduced her working hours so she could help care for their grandchildren while their parents worked full-time.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"They couldn't have managed five days a week childcare. It's so expensive today," Catherine told SBS's Insight.

"So to look after the children, that's a saving in hundreds of dollars for them."

There may be no money changing hands, but the arrangement has significant financial value.

And Shane and Catherine are part of a much bigger, and often largely invisible, flow of support between Australian generations.

What is the 'Booster Economy'?

New research from SBS CulturalConnect estimates older Australians provide more than $140 billion worth of everyday financial support to younger family members each year.

The research involved in-depth interviews with 50 parents and grandparents providing support, followed by a survey of around 2,500 Australians.

More than 12 million Australians were found to support younger adult family members in some way.

Researchers have dubbed it the "Booster Economy", or the wealth and financial support flowing between generations while parents and grandparents are still alive.

And it extends far beyond the familiar "Bank of Mum and Dad" helping children into the housing market.

Among those providing support, 34 per cent had bought groceries for younger family members, 33 per cent had paid for restaurant meals and 30 per cent had bought clothes.

Almost one in five had paid for travel, while 14 per cent had bought a car and the same proportion had purchased appliances or electronics.

Forty-two per cent had provided cash, while 19 per cent had helped pay off debt.

The $140 billion estimate excludes cash transfers, debt repayments, homes and home deposits, capturing instead the scale of everyday purchases being made by older Australians for younger family members.

The Bank of Mum and Dad is getting bigger

Finder personal finance expert Sarah Megginson said its research suggests reliance on family wealth is already growing significantly in one of the biggest areas of household finances: housing.

Finder recently found 30 per cent of homeowners surveyed had received family assistance to purchase their property.

Contributions towards a deposit were the most common form of support, while 8 per cent said their family had paid for their home outright.

But Megginson said the change over time was particularly striking.

"About four years ago, those stats were looking like 10 per cent — like one in 10 were getting help from their parents," she told SBS News.

"Last year it came back around 20 per cent ... and now we're at three in 10.

"So we've just seen that trend continue to get even deeper year on year."

Megginson said older Australians were increasingly seeing the financial pressures facing their children and grandchildren and reconsidering when they passed on their wealth.

"Instead of the more traditional path of leaving an inheritance after they've gone, they've actually started, I guess, releasing it early," she said.

While housing deposits were a major example, Megginson said parents were also contributing towards expenses such as private school fees and other significant lifestyle costs.

From inheritance to everyday expenses

Megginson said the financial relationship between parents and their adult children had also changed considerably within a generation.

"I'm in my 40s, and I moved out and bought my first home in my early 20s, and that was the end of any kind of money relationship with my parents," she said.

"I was a grown-up then, paid for all of my own things."

But Megginson said younger colleagues in their 20s and 30s had described parents continuing to pay for things such as restaurant meals, or covering the cost of their children and their partners joining family holidays.

"I think that has been a huge generational shift," she said.

Housing affordability was one of the major forces behind the change, Megginson said, with the gap between incomes and property prices widening significantly over recent decades.

The report by Financial Services Council proposes changes that would see the amount of superannuation benefits left each year as a bequest halved by 2060, ensuring superannuation is primarily used up as income for retirement. Source: AAP / Moodboard

She said she increasingly heard from Australians who believed that without an inheritance or help from their parents, they would "simply never own a home".

Finder research has also found one in 10 Australians say they will need an inheritance to achieve a major financial goal, such as buying a property.

What if your parents can't afford to help?

But access to the Booster Economy is far from universal.

The SBS research highlights a stark difference between younger Australians whose families can provide significant support and those without the same financial safety net — including some who instead provide support to older relatives.

The consequences can extend beyond the immediate value of the help.

Regular free childcare, for example, can save a family hundreds of dollars a week while allowing parents to remain in the workforce. Help with groceries or bills can leave more income available for other expenses, while a home deposit can provide a pathway into a property market that might otherwise be out of reach.

Megginson said she grew up in a family that lived "pay to pay", without generational wealth to pass down.

"If you don't have generational wealth coming your way, if you're not lucky enough to be one of those 8 per cent of people who have got a house bought for them, what can you do to try and build wealth for yourself and get yourself in a better financial position?" she said.

Is financial independence changing?

Australia is also approaching a massive transfer of accumulated wealth, with previous estimates suggesting Australians aged over 60 could pass around $3.5 trillion to younger generations over two decades.

But the Booster Economy suggests some of that transfer is already happening — one grocery shop, childcare day and house deposit at a time.

Megginson believes financial pressures could even change how Australians think about independence.

While adult children remaining at home well into their 20s can sometimes be viewed as having failed to "fly the nest", she noted multigenerational living is already commonplace in many cultures.

READ MORE The taboo wealth tax debate experts say Australia can no longer ignore

"We might see a trend that is driven by finances to more embrace that style of living," she said.

"It might have some of those cultural benefits, and ... the whole 'it takes a village to raise a family' philosophy might start to flourish a little bit more."

For some Australians, that village is increasingly providing an economic safety net too — one that can look very different depending on the family you're born into.

title: Death of the auction? Sellers move to private sales in softening market
text:
in brief New data from Domain suggests more property sellers have moved away from auctions to private treaty sales.

The property platform has also found a rise in listings starting as private treaty.

Property sellers are increasingly moving away from the traditional auction in response to a softening housing market, new data from Domain suggests, with experts arguing that Australia has firmly entered a "buyer's market".

The online property platform has found a sharp rise in listings initially slated for auction being converted to private treaty in capital cities. Across Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane, Adelaide and Canberra, the average proportion sales that are auctions has more than doubled from 29.6 per cent in February to 60.8 per cent in July.

Listings starting as private treaty also increased at the same time, highlighting a substantial move away from reliance on auction-day results as sellers seek the best price for their asset.

Domain's chief of economics and research, Nicola Powell, told SBS News that this shift in seller behaviour reflects the softening market conditions "unravelling across the nation".

"Many sellers are testing the market and realising that there just isn't that buyer depth there anymore," she said.

After major post-pandemic growth and following decades of steady increases, the Australian property market has seen a broad downturn over winter.

Data from property analyst Cotality shows that, while Sydney and Melbourne began to slow at the start of the year, national house price values peaked in March and have declined 3.6 per cent since.

Powell argued spring will likely be slower than usual, with Domain predicting property prices will continue to fall through the rest of the year.

"I think what we're going to see from buyers is they are going to want to get that greater value for money," she said.

The second quarter of 2026 saw the first sustained decline in national housing stock value since 2022, with Australian Bureau of Statistics figures showing a 0.3 per cent drop or $34.1 billion.

Auctions still a good idea

Shannan Whitney, co-founder of prominent Sydney property group BresicWhitney, told SBS News that shying away from auction sales could be the wrong move for sellers.

"Pricing tends to be more in line with where the market needs to be in an auction process than it does in a for sale process," he said.

"I think more vendors will be more comfortable with auction in Sydney over the next three or four months, but it just takes a little bit of time for everyone to work through the cycle."

Whitney expects the property cycle is now through its "first third" after months of price adjustments. It's "natural", he said, for sellers to want to retreat into non-auction sales where they feel safer or more in control during such a period, which he believes is now levelling off in Sydney.

"Vendors genuinely contemplating a sale are now much more aligned and educated about where the market is," he said. "Therefore, we think we expect to see clearance rates probably go up and improve over the next four months."

Sellers who aren't "in line" with the market should consider their position and perhaps pause on a sale for the next 12 months to three years, Whitney advised.

Buyers, on the other hand, are experiencing very favourable conditions. However, Whitney suggested that waiting and expecting prices to continue to drop might not be the best strategy.

Even though the market was soft, trading was better now compared with earlier in the year.

"What we're seeing now is much more engagement from buyers where they see pricing at reasonable, viable levels," he said. "We are seeing properties sell quicker now than we did six months ago."

Rapid corrections

Sustained high borrowing costs and stubborn inflation are some of the key drivers squeezing buyer affordability. At the same time, the surge in listings through autumn and winter forced national average clearance rates down to around 46 per cent.

"Listings have risen, choice is better than it once was, and particularly in markets like Sydney and Melbourne, it is very much a buyer's market," Powell said.

Economists note clearance rates below 60 per cent reduce inflationary pressure on house prices.

Major financial institutions including Commonwealth Bank have forecast a peak-to-trough decline in house prices of 8 to 10 per cent, with the market expected to hit its bottom in early 2027.

Those in the market are already pricing in the changed conditions, Whitney said, noting that the speed of information transfer at present means adjustments and property cycles happen far more quickly than they used to.

The Reserve Bank of Australia is widely expected to raise interest rates for the fourth time this year during its meeting at the end of this month. With an increased cash rate of 4.6 per cent, buyer confidence is expected to take a further hit.

If the RBA does increase rates this month, it is likely to trigger a continued "drag on inventory" as conditions slow even further.

"The cycle for buyers will lengthen and look more favourable," Whitney said.

title: 'Disfiguring': Behind the growing spread of a flesh-eating ulcer
text: In brief Buruli ulcer cases have spread beyond coastal Victoria, with new clusters reported in Melbourne suburbs. Researching are racing to find new ways to prevent the spread. Warmer weather has arrived, and mosquitoes will be buzzing about before you know it. As El Niño is expected to bring an early start to summer heat, it’s likely mosquitoes will make their presence felt earlier than usual. The threat of mosquitoes depositing flesh-eating bacteria has been restricted to a few parts of the country. But while rare, research shows it is now showing up in more areas — including in backyards in Melbourne’s inner city. So what exactly is Buruli ulcer, where is it now found, and how can you prevent it? Here’s what we know so far, and what researchers are currently developing to protect against the bacteria in future. What are Buruli ulcers? Buruli ulcer is a skin infection resulting from the bacterium Mycobacterium ulcerans. News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS. It starts as small and often painless inflammation after a mosquito bite, which may not be seen until months after initial infection. It transforms into a disfiguring ulcer after many weeks. If left untreated, it can continue increasing in size with a loss of skin and muscle. A buruli ulcer is treated with an eight-week course of antibiotics. Recovery can be much slower than expected for other common skin infections, with healing time highly dependent on the condition of the ulcer when first treated. It may take more than four months for ulcers to heal. How do people become infected? Mycobacterium ulcerans can infect urban wildlife, such as possums, which suffer symptoms similar to those in humans. Recent research has shown mosquitoes pass the bacterium to people. The mosquito most closely associated with areas at risk of Mycobacterium ulcerans is Aedes notoscriptus. Commonly known as the Australian backyard mosquito, it is widespread in Australia and commonly found in water-holding containers in suburban areas. There may be other pathways of infection, but health authorities have strongly encouraged people to prevent mosquito bites as the best way to avoid Buruli ulcer. Where is it found? Buruli ulcer has been reported in more than 30 countries around the world, including in Africa, South America and the Western Pacific. In Australia, it has been reported in several states, territories and regions, including Victoria, Far North Queensland, the Northern Territory and New South Wales. Victoria has been hit hardest, with 426 cases reported in the state in 2025 alone. Victorian cases have mostly been reported from coastal regions, but Melbourne’s suburbs have also seen an increase in activity. Inner north-west suburbs such as Essendon, Brunswick West and Moonee Ponds are part of the new cluster. With the potential for more cases, and in more locations, surveillance beyond known areas of activity is needed. Since Buruli ulcer became a notifiable disease in NSW, there have been six cases reported from the NSW south coast. There was concern this was because the Victorian outbreak had spread to the state and could also spread to new regions. But genomic analysis suggests the NSW cases are from a separate outbreak rather than spread from Victoria. This raises questions about how widespread this pathogen may be and what conditions are likely to give rise to human infections in new regions. How best to stop the flesh-eating bacteria’s spread? Australian health authorities have recommended insect repellents and reducing exposure to mosquitoes for decades to reduce the risks of mosquito-borne disease. But while health authorities might ordinarily consider insecticides to control mosquito populations, they’re not likely to be an effective way to reduce numbers of mosquitoes buzzing about the local suburbs in the long term. New research in Victoria led by two of us (Véronique Paris and Andrew Buultjens) tested a novel approach to mosquito control and found evidence that reducing mosquito numbers can also reduce a person’s risk of contracting Buruli ulcer. Using mosquitoes as pest-controllers Special devices, known as autodissemination stations, are designed to offer a breeding site to mosquitoes looking for somewhere to lay their eggs. A stinky mix of water and yeast draws them in. Once inside, the mosquito is exposed to a gauze strip coated with the control agent pyriproxyfen (an insect growth regulator) and Beauveria bassiana (insect specific fungus). When the mosquito leaves the station, its days are numbered due to the fungal infection. But before they die, they’ll transfer the mosquito control agent to other water-holding containers as they look for other places to lay their eggs. The mosquitoes become accidental pest controllers themselves. How effective was it? After eight weeks of station deployment, mosquito egg counts (a measure of mosquito activity) were 70% lower in treatment areas compared with control areas. Buruli ulcer presents an unusual challenge when trying to measure whether an intervention had impact on human disease because symptoms typically develop almost five months after infection. To account for this delay, we had to work backwards to estimate when infection likely occurred and use forensic genomic analysis to determine which cases were acquired locally. At the predicted peak of the mosquito-control effect, Buruli ulcer incidence was estimated to be 83 per cent lower in the treatment areas than in the control areas. The greater the reduction in mosquitoes, the greater the apparent protection from Buruli ulcer, providing further evidence that mosquito control can reduce disease risk. The mosquito control stations used in the study are not yet available for purchase in Australia, but regulatory approval for their use is imminent, and new products using similar approaches are also being tested. However, in this study the control stations were deployed in high numbers, so it’s unclear what the impact of their use in a single household would be. So how can you reduce your risk of Buruli ulcer this summer? Current predictions are for hot and relatively dry conditions this summer in eastern Australia. While this may mean there are fewer mosquitoes emerging from wetlands and other bodies of water, the mosquitoes closely associated with Mycobacterium ulcerans spread are found in our backyards. Water will still be available for mosquitoes around the home in bird baths, rainwater tanks, blocked drains, sump pits and roof gutters, and water left out for wildlife. To prevent mosquitoes from breeding in them, make sure you refill bird baths weekly, clear your gutters, cover water tanks, and empty and refill water for wildlife at least once per week. It’s also a good idea to keep using insect repellents. Mosquito control, whatever form it takes, will never get rid of all the mosquitoes. Covering up with long-sleeve shirts, long pants and enclosed shoes when outdoors will also help stop the bites. title: Devastating, funny, heartbreaking and hopeful – RECLAIM was one of the best dance events in years
text:
State Library of NSW, September 11

The Mitchell Library’s colonial splendour is wreathed in ceremonial smoke when I arrive: ornate moulded walls, towering bookshelves, spiral stairs leading to elevated balconies and soaring skylights crowning a vast central reading space.

Here, amid the books, drawers, and antique reading tables, dance legend Stephen Page is back with a site-specific premiere. The former Bangarra Dance Theatre artistic director wields his fellowship with the State Library of NSW in RECLAIM: A Contemporary Ceremony, co-written with Alana Valentine for the library’s 200th anniversary.

A scene from RECLAIM: A Contemporary Ceremony, co-written by Stephen Page with Alana Valentine at the State Library of NSW for the library’s 200th anniversary. Daniel Boud

Damien Cooper’s stage lights illuminate and the shelves seem to fade under fingers of sunlight and tree branches, the plasterwork receding beneath lapping coastal waves. The air comes alive with Steve Francis’s soundscape of birds, crackling fire and haunting Indigenous song, joined by the plaintive strains of Taj Pigram’s voice and mandolin.

The performers sweep onstage in ceremonial dance, singing and bearing leaves as light rays fall behind them like a setting sun. The impact is immediate, uncanny and unspeakably beautiful: the library’s familiar architecture superimposed with an overwhelming evocation of Country and memory. It is like being gifted second sight, the library fracturing into palpable layers of time and meaning before your eyes, each layer simultaneously visible and powerful.

In Protest, actors Brendon Boney, Angeline Penrith and Dalara Williams trace the work of generations of Indigenous advocates. Daniel Boud

Seven scenes follow, the audience gazing through the centuries at a crescendo of storytelling: by turns warm, devastating, funny, heartbreaking and hopeful.

In Place, Indigenous engagement librarian Melissa Jackson speaks from a balcony about the library’s decolonisation work, followed by Bradley Smith’s searing solo as an Indigenous man reduced to a collected “specimen”.

A scene from the work, which was warm, devastating, funny, heartbreaking and hopeful. Daniel Boud

In Protest, actors Brendon Boney, Angeline Penrith and Dalara Williams in early 20th-century costume (Jennifer Irwin’s designs) are assembled beneath a banner, megaphone in hand, tracing generations of Indigenous advocates. Their true stories will make your eyes sting with tears.

An excerpt from Page’s Patyegarang pairs Smith and Buia David in a gorgeously romantic duet about the first historical colonial-Indigenous exchange of Dharug language. Preen has Penrith comically auditioning to play Matthew Flinders’ cat; and Protect warms with a storytelling tribute to Mum Shirl.

The evening emotionally detonates with Presence, the devastating final scene from Page’s Bennelong. The stage blazes with Beau Dean Riley Smith, reprising the eponymous role he originated, his electric limbs seemingly thrown together and torn apart by tectonic external forces, his face caught between surprise and pain. The concluding image – Riley Smith crying out as he is walled up alive in a white sepulchre – is every bit as poetic and horrifying as at its premiere almost a decade ago.

Somehow, these vignettes never feel like a Page jukebox. Page turns his extraordinary body of work into another kind of archive, placing past choreography beside living testimony, new theatrical scenes, historical storytelling, and the library’s own collection until each illuminates the others. RECLAIM is site-specific work in the fullest sense: it changes how you see the building itself.

At the finish, the audience leaps to its feet with a roar. Unmissable, and one of the best dance events in years.

It’s been 15 long years, but the Wests Tigers are finally playing finals football again. For the first time since 2011, a top-grade Tigers team will play a match at the business end of the season, thanks to the club’s NRLW side sealing a top-four finish with a 7-4 record during the 11-match regular season. Wests Tigers captain Kezie Apps has been with the team since their inaugural year in 2022. George Chan It’s an impressive turnaround for a team that finished with just one win, and the wooden spoon for the second year in a row in 2025. One of the most significant changes for the NRLW team this year has been the arrival of coach Craig Sandercock. “If you were to say to me at the start of the year, you’re playing finals footy, I would have 100 per cent taken that,” Sandercock said. Wests Tigers NRLW coach Craig Sandercock. NRL Images “It’s been a great, great year, and you could probably consider it a really successful year from the club, especially with where we’ve come from.” The team always had potential, said Sandercock, but there were a handful of areas that required improvement.

“When I watched all their games from last year, they only won one game, but there were periods in every game that they competed, and they competed hard, and it was just, I suppose, some key moments last year that really cost them,” Sandercock said. “Then that fed into that mindset of, here we go again, and then they concede another try and another try. “We’ve still got our young girls coming through who are learning and who are going really good, but we’ve also got that great balance of the leaders and the experience within the group as well. “It’s obviously been a big change this year from going from only winning one game last year, and now here we are near finals, and we’ve come fourth. “Reflecting on the season that we’ve had ... and comparing that to last year coming last and then coming fourth, I think that’s something that needs to be celebrated and something that needs to be recognised of how hard the girls have worked to get to where we are.” The Tigers will play either Newcastle, who they beat with a 68th-minute field goal in round eight, or Canberra, who they lost 22-10 to in the final round of the season, in week one of the finals.

title: Sharks boss says it’s time to end ‘embarrassing’ stadium debate. Even if that means defeat

Cronulla chief executive Dino Mezzatesta fears the Sharks may never host an NRL final in their own backyard again, but says the NRL should implement a blanket finals policy that will ensure all clubs are treated the same. The Sharks’ 26-16 defeat of North Queensland at Allianz Stadium was attended by an official crowd of 17,429 on Saturday night, only around 2500 more than the capacity of Cronulla’s regular home ground, Ocean Protect Stadium. Loading Under discretionary powers outlined to NRL clubs at the start of the season, the ARLC retains the right to decide where week one finals are played, chiefly to ensure fans aren’t locked out of smaller venues like Sydney’s boutique stadiums. The NRL opted to move the qualifying final between the Sharks and the Cowboys to Allianz Stadium, but the underwhelming crowd on Saturday prompted yet another round of debate around the Cronulla club’s right to host finals.

Advertisement

Star halfback Nicho Hynes appeared to question the NRL’s decision to shift the game, telling Channel Nine that while he was not blaming Sharks fans, he found it “upsetting, disappointing and embarrassing there’s so many free seats here”. Mezzatesta and Sharks officials have stridently argued for Cronulla’s earned right to host a home final in the Shire over several recent seasons. North Queensland’s Braidon Burns scores in front of plenty of empty seats at Allianz Stadium. Getty Images But given the NRL’s decision to move Saturday’s match against the traditionally low-drawing out-of-town Cowboys to Moore Park, Mezzatesta responded to the modest crowd by calling on the governing body to now make it a level playing field and scrap the discretionary aspect. “I’m still disappointed because nothing will change the fact that we earned the right to play that home semi-final at our home ground,” Mezzatesta said on Sunday.

Advertisement

“But maybe we’re at the point where you have to change that rule for everyone then. Just play the semis at all the big stadiums from here on, regardless of who is in. “If you’re a Sydney team, you’re playing at Allianz, Accor [Stadium] or Commbank [Stadium]. If you’re in Queensland, you play at Suncorp [Stadium] and if you’re in New Zealand, then you play at Eden [Park]. Ocean Protect Stadium has various issues holding it back from hosting NRL finals. Harry Breen “I don’t mean to disadvantage other clubs, but we have this discussion every year around finals venues every year, and to me, if you’re not going to let us play at our home ground, then lock in the big venues and take the guessing games and the controversy out of it.” Mezzatesta’s suggestion would mean Sydney clubs like Manly (Four Pines Park), St George Illawarra (Kogarah and WIN Stadium) and Wests Tigers (Leichhardt Oval and Campbelltown Stadium) would also not have the ability to play finals at their suburban home grounds.

Advertisement

The NRL on Sunday announced that next week’s Warriors-Knights semi-final will be played at Auckland’s Eden Park, which can accommodate around 24,000 more supporters than Go Media Stadium. Given the NRL collects gate takings of all finals matches, at an average of $50 per finals ticket, that represents a windfall of around $1.5 million for the governing body. Warriors fans have good reason to be in full voice this year. Getty Despite the Warriors selling out their surprise week-one loss to the Dolphins in a reported 17 minutes last week, the NRL’s two finals crowds at Allianz Stadium have underwhelmed after another year of strong attendances. South Sydney’s first post-season game since 2022 against the Knights on Friday night drew only 28,152, while the Sharks-Cowboys clash amounted to less than half the venue’s seats being filled.

Advertisement

The presence of big-drawing clubs Canterbury and Brisbane made for bumper crowds and eight of nine finals games being sold out last season (albeit with Shark Park one of those). Related Article NRL 2026 Fans stay home but Sharks turn up to end Cowboys’ season The Dolphins’ maiden preliminary final appearance and Warriors return to Eden Park are expected to draw 50,000-strong crowds in coming weeks. As for the Sharks, Mezzatesta believes there is still scope to host a home final against interstate opposition rivals like the Cowboys or Titans next year – if the ARLC’s discretionary rules remain. But until Ocean Protect Stadium gets a much-needed upgrade to improve its tired facilities, even that prospect appears slim.

“There’s still a place for suburban grounds in our game,” he said. “We know our facilities need improvements, and we will continue to pursue government funding and Peter V’landys is a big supporter of us doing that. “And once the stadium is back fully online with a capacity of 18,000, well, the discussion around finals changes again. We could argue depending on who our opponent is, that there’s reason to host at a suburban ground again. “But really, I’m now thinking if you want to play all the big games at the big venues from now on, well then be done with it and make it the same rule for everyone.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday. text:

Exclusive NationalVictoriaGo west Phil wanted to rent a shop in Footscray. The owner would rather it sits empty Cassandra Morgan September 13, 2026 — 1:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

During five years’ trading in Melbourne’s west, Phil Gaby’s business has had just as many homes. Nan’s Bakehouse began at the markets, then moved to Footscray Plaza before expanding into the business next door. A coffee van followed, then a new store in Moonee Ponds – before its closure, when they ran into financial strife. Nan’s Bakehouse owner Phil Gaby said many landlords in the area would rather keep their shops vacant than have them occupied by businesses. Chris Hopkins Despite failure and two evictions, Nan’s endures in Footscray – one of Melbourne’s toughest places for businesses to thrive, a new Property Council of Australia report suggests. But Gaby said he wouldn’t want to be anywhere else.

Advertisement

“After we failed at Moonee Ponds, I realised that success meant the community and the people,” he said. “Even our store now has been held together by people from our old store, continually following us around because they believe in the same things we do.” The Nicholson Street Mall in Footscray, which is home to the former Forges site, alongside many vacant shopfronts. Joe Armao Despite a $1.5 billion investment in the new Footscray Hospital – and millions more in transport, education, and sporting and social infrastructure – the inner-city suburb has stalled, the Property Council found in its Revitalising Victoria’s priority precincts report, in large part due to land banking. “I applied for one place on Barkly Street, and it has been empty for two years now … The owner said he did not want to spend any money, and he’d rather leave it sitting empty,” Gaby said.

Advertisement

Related Article Go west This western suburb is ripe for a housing boom, council says. Developers disagree “He was concerned that, if the business went bad, then that’s his loss. That’s how he looked at it. Whereas before, a landlord would look at it as an investment.” Footscray’s land banking issue is symptomatic of a more complex problem, whereby high construction costs, elevated taxes and charges, expensive finance and subdued apartment values are deterring landowners from developing projects, the Property Council found. New apartments in Footscray average $100,000 less than Melbourne’s median apartment price, making it difficult for developers to justify new builds when construction costs remain high, KPMG urban economist Terry Rawnsley said. High costs were also accompanied by a 1297 per cent increase in approved dwellings in central Footscray in the 2022-23 financial year, compared with the previous year (908 dwellings from 65).

Advertisement

A similar pattern emerged in the 2024-25 financial year (with 704 approved dwellings, compared to the previous year’s 38), helping to keep prices down. Related Article City life Violence, nostalgia and the unravelling of Melbourne’s first pedestrian mall The Property Council suggests that if prices continue to fall with federal tax changes, this could be replicated across Melbourne and undermine the feasibility of new projects. “Developers are likely to be holding sites and waiting for feasibility to improve,” Rawnsley told The Age. “That could come through stronger sale prices, as the existing apartment supply is absorbed, although there is little indication that construction costs will fall materially in the foreseeable future.”

Advertisement

However, the report warns a “business-as-usual” approach, even with continued local and state government investment, won’t be enough to fix the issues in Footscray. “Getting Footscray right would not only unlock a major opportunity for Melbourne’s west,” Property Council Victorian executive director Cath Evans said. “It could provide a blueprint for how Victoria can turn its broader activity centre and precinct ambitions into reality.” The former Forges site at Nicholson Street Mall in Footscray. Joe Armao The Property Council is urging the state government to commit to a six-step plan to haul Footscray out of its slump, pointing to vacant shopfronts, deteriorating buildings and “hoarded” development sites. The council names the former Forges site, Little Saigon Market, Paint Spot, Kinnear’s Ropeworks, the former bus depot and the former Belgravia Hotel among them, and notes each has their own “commercial circumstances” – but they collectively represent “a significant volume of unrealised housing, employment, activation and public realm challenges”.

Advertisement

At a forum in Footscray making the case for Maribyrnong City Council’s $148 million Creative West arts precinct project last month, Mayor Mohamed Semra described the former Forges site as a once-thriving retail destination, since “left to decay for 17 years”. The report suggests more should be done to capitalise on the arts precinct project, as well as other investments. Related Article City life The old hospital that’s become a battleground in Melbourne’s west The Property Council encouraged government to prioritise improving Footscray’s streetscapes and begin demolition programs to remove derelict or condemned buildings. The state government should also look at waving or reducing taxes and levies for developers building in Footscray and other Melbourne activity centres, tying incentives to timelines or community infrastructure, the Property Council said.

Advertisement

Government should also consider public-private partnerships for big development sites, dedicate a department or area of council to getting a move on big projects, and better coordinate local support services to shore up faith in Footscray’s safety, the report said. Semra said Maribyrnong Council was working to improve Footscray’s safety, amenity and shopfronts, support economic development, and draw people to local attractions and events. He said his council would consider the Property Council’s report. “We’re working collaboratively with landowners, businesses, community organisations, and state and federal governments to speed up action on vacant sites in the Footscray CBD.” The Victorian government pointed to its investment in Footscray’s health, education, transport, sport and community infrastructure. A government spokesperson said that “through planning certainty, infrastructure investment and better transport connections”, the government was helping unlock the area’s growth. They are feature films you will almost certainly never see. Made for comically small budgets. Starring no-one you know. Yet at a time when even well-funded Australian films regularly struggle to find an audience, young filmmakers keep making ultra-low budget features, even if it means using up their savings, going into debt and burning favours from friends and acquaintances. “It was always probably my biggest dream to just be in a movie” said actor-writer-director Jonah Erofeyeff (left) with actor Madeleine Walker and actor-writer-director Emrah Akbulut, who made the feature film Where The Sky Meets The Ground for $15,000. Sitthixay Ditthavong Many will never make another film. So why do it? “It was always probably my biggest dream to just be in a movie,” Jonah Erofeyeff, 21, says. “You look up on the big screen and sort of see yourself there.”

Advertisement

Related Article Cinema Armie Hammer is back after being cancelled. But his choice of film is problematic He was not just thinking about himself. Erofeyeff made Where The Sky Meets The Ground with close friend Emrah Akbulut, 21, after meeting at an acting course. It’s a drama about four friends who have one last adventure before uni finishes – trekking into the bush to find a crashed plane supposedly carrying drugs. Akbulut was watching the ’80s classic Stand By Me one night when he realised he had shared similar friendships. Inspired by Stand By Me: Jonah Erofeyeff and Emrah Akbulut’s film Where The Sky Meets The Ground Mach 10

Advertisement

“I messaged Jonah as the credits were rolling, and I was like, ‘This is a movie we can make – modernise it and make it Australian, authentic to us’,” he says. Adds Erofeyeff: “We’re both actors. We wanted to just make a project for us to act in – a feature film with heaps of scenes.” So the duo made the film – jointly writing, directing, starring and financing it – with $15,000 of their savings. Erofeyeff was working in maintenance at theme park Raging Waters (now Sydney Action Park); Akbulut was packaging wool in a warehouse before moving into baggage handling at Sydney Airport. They kept down costs on the shoot by calling on friends from their acting classes and Erofeyeff’s filmmaking course at Randwick TAFE for the cast and crew, car pooling to set and bringing snack bags for everyone. “Should I put a deposit on a house or should I make a film?“: Adrian Ortega largely self-funded the feature film Westgate, with Sarah Nicolazzo, who plays a single mother still carrying trauma from the bridge collapse in 1970. Simon Schluter

Advertisement

When their film was knocked back by festivals and distributors, the duo paid for their own premiere at the Randwick Ritz, gambling – successfully as it turned out – that they could cover the $5000 cost with ticket sales. They are now hoping to make another film. “The main dream is acting, but we always have that drive to make something else,” Akbulut says. “Even if it’s not a full production, we just want to be behind the camera, in front of the camera, doing something.” Sarah Nicolazzo and Max Nappo in Adrian Ortega’s Westgate. Proud Wing Melbourne editor and filmmaking teacher Adrian Ortega was 25 when he shot his first feature film, the comic drama Cerulean Blue, about an introvert (Jack Michel) picking up a high-spirited hitchhiker (Senie Priti), in 2017.

Advertisement

He self-financed it with $35,000 to $40,000 from his savings as a waiter at the Footscray Community Arts Centre cafe and considered it a success when Cerulean Blue premiered at Melbourne International Film Festival in 2019 then was picked up by streaming service Stan. “It didn’t break even because we played festivals and then, when it premiered in late 2019, COVID happened,” he says. “But it developed a name for myself in the industry to be able to get other projects made.” Related Article Cinema Indian films out-perform Australian releases at the local box office Two years ago, Ortega tried Victorian state film agency VicScreen but ended up self-financing his second feature, Westgate, too. It cost $85,000: $70,000 from his savings and the rest from crowdfunding and supporters. “I thought ‘should I put a deposit on a house or should I make a film?’,” he says. “I chose film again.”

Advertisement

Set over 24 hours in 1999, Westgate is a drama about an Italian-Australian single mother (Sarah Nicolazzo) from West Footscray who still carries the trauma from her father being killed in the West Gate Bridge collapse in 1970. It was a personal story for Ortega, 34, who grew up in an Italian/Spanish migrant family in Footscray. “It’s basically my mother’s story,” he says. “Sarah’s basically playing a version of my mother and Julian (Max Nappo) is basically a young version of me.” After premiering at MIFF and screening at SXSW Sydney last year, Westgate had a modest cinema run, was released on DVD and Blu-ray and is now streaming on Prime Video and Apple TV. While it is yet to break even, Ortega thinks it will with more sales over time. He is now planning another feature film but with a difference. “I’d love to not spend my own money on a third one,” he says.

Advertisement

Screen Australia’s latest drama report showed that 34 Australian films, including Westgate, started shooting in 2024-25. While 22 of them cost $1 million-$10 million, three cost less than $1 million. War Machine has been a Netflix hit but only The Travellers ($2 million) and Leviticus ($1.5 million) have made an impact in cinemas so far. That aligns with the findings of Nick Hayes’ recent report Made Not Seen: Australians go to cinemas in large numbers, but Australian film attendance has collapsed to the point where Indian releases are now more successful at the local box office. title: Joyous energy and raucous humour collide in this five-star gig
text:
Advertisement

Key points MUSIC: Belle and Sebastian perform If You’re Feeling Sinister at the Palais

OPERA: Lyric Opera perform a Regency-Era Serse at the Gasworks Theatre

DANCE: 7 Dances for 7 People is performed at Northcote Town Hall

MUSIC

Belle and Sebastian ★★★★★

Palais Theatre, September 12 “Welcome to the second recording session for this still quite-new band,” Stuart Murdoch says with a grin. His tongue is firmly in cheek – Belle and Sebastian, the indie-pop group he’s led for more than half his life, is on tour celebrating its 30th year. In 1996, the bookish Scots made their debut with two albums: Tigermilk and If You’re Feeling Sinister. On this anniversary tour, they’re alternating playing those records in full. Melbourne gets the Sinister treatment. Belle & Sebastian perform at the Palais, September 12, 2026. Richard Clifford Playing albums in full live can be a cynical cash-cow in the age of commodified nostalgia, but there’s no denying the sheer delight of hearing a beloved album like this in all its glory. On record, Sinister’s arrangements are delicate; live, they’re injected with a shot of joyous energy, with buzzing synth to boot. Many of these songs begin with Murdoch alone, singing with that sweet, instantly recognisable voice, before the eight other musicians on stage slowly blossom to create sunlight in musical form. Lead guitarist Stevie Jackson raucously takes on the harmonica for Me and the Major, his movements a chaotic blur.

Advertisement

As the album reaches its halfway point, a projection behind the band shows the LP being flipped on a turntable – “a bit of antiquated attention to detail,” Murdoch says. Eager fans have been dancing in the aisles from the beginning, but when the band plays Get Me Away, I’m Dying, the entire venue is on its feet. The gorgeous Mayfly is another highlight from this half, but really, it’s all joy, not least because Murdoch and co are clearly having a blast, too. Murdoch’s signature humour is on display all night as he intersperses the music with quips, including a spiel about Victoria’s slogans as seen on number plates and a joke about Viagra as he takes his medication on stage. “Back to sweetness and light!” he says, and back they go. Sarah Martin, Stuart Murdoch and Stevie Jackson of Belle & Sebastian. Richard Clifford A guitar-heavy I’m a Cuckoo kicks off the second set, comprising songs from the rest of the band’s long career. Belle and Sebastian have such a varied discography that it’s a grab-bag every night. There are some deeper cuts here, such as 2010’s Little Lou, Ugly Jack, Prophet John, recorded with Norah Jones; here, it’s long-time vocalist Sarah Martin who does the honours, beautiful as ever. 2006’s Funny Little Frog is a charming, nostalgic treat. The band is pulling songs out on the fly by the end, with Another Sunny Day closing the night. It’s apt – with 30 years of sunny days up their sleeves, Belle and Sebastian keep on delivering.

Reviewed by Giselle Au-Nhien Nguyen

Advertisement

OPERA

Serse ★★

Gasworks Theatre, until September 13 We’re all getting restless. Twenty minutes after the curtain was meant to go up for the opening show of Lyric Opera’s Serse, we’re still waiting for the conductor to raise his baton. Eventually, company artistic director and conductor Patrick Burns addresses the audience, explaining that though they’ve tried to fix the issue, they’ve had no success. Baroque opera has a small but loyal audience in Melbourne Jodie Hutchinson Both projectors have died. For the near-three-hour Italian opera we’re about to witness, there will be no surtitles. No translations. Oh dear. Turns out, if it was sung in English, it’d be hard to follow anyway. Handel’s 1738 opera about the King of Persia is one of those operas stacked with couples pursuing, deceiving, rejecting and reuniting with one another, plus disguises and mistaken identities thrown in, of course.

Advertisement

Baroque opera has a small but loyal audience in Melbourne, but for a company that has commendably programmed contemporary operas in previous seasons, Serse is, frankly, an odd choice. The production, by director Beng Oh and designer Christina Logan-Bell, is certainly clever, updated to the Regency era where it fits quite well, what with all the letter-writing and love-in-turmoil. But even with tech issues aside, faults remain. The ornamentation demands were too much for some, and the approach (though it is correct Baroque style) of leaving out vibrato resulted in some unenergised vocal patches. The production, by director Beng Oh and designer Christina Logan-Bell, is certainly clever. Jodie Hutchinson Some shined, like mezzo Naomi Flatman, who with a honeyed, resonant sound, delivered the standout performance of the night. Soprano Rebecca Rashleigh too gave a consistently vibrant performance, with thrilling top notes. As Serse, it was testament to Sally-Anne Russell’s comedic talent that though we mostly had no idea what was going on, people still laughed when they were, presumably, meant to. Though it was the initial problem, the ensuing convoluted plot, repetitive musical style and uneven singing proved that being sung in a foreign language is not the greatest measure of an opera’s accessibility.

Reviewed by Bridget Davies

Advertisement

DANCE

7 Dances for 7 People ★★★

Northcote Town Hall, until September 19 Yes, there are indeed seven dances – or sections – in choreographer Trá Mi Dinh’s latest work, but only the first of them is unambiguously successful. I would happily have watched this strange, lustrous gambit for the full hour, either extended or simply repeated. Tra Mi Dinh and Rachel Coulson in 7 Dances for 7 People. Darren Gill Two dancers emerge from billowing clouds of smoke, like figures in a dream, amid an eerie tintinnabulation. Delicate unison stepping gives their progress toward the audience an insect-like grace; raised arms and joined hands further heighten their otherworldly appearance. The awkward position of the arms, which restricts the movement of the upper body, creates a sense of fragility and risk. It’s as if their grip on one another is all that prevents them tumbling back in the cloud of smoke. It gives the whole scene a shimmery, slippery sort of ephemerality.

Advertisement

After the first dance, the movement becomes more eclectic. Smooth isolations, with their tensing and releasing, give way to looser spinning figures. Vaguely balletic poses contrast with thrusting modern dance gestures. And everything whirls together in the smoke. The combinations are not always compelling, but something of the mysterious atmosphere of the first section persists. And interesting details register throughout, particularly in the way the seven dancers move between pairs and trios, with new arrangement materialising in the gloom. The balletic poses contrast with modern dance gestures as everything whirls together amid the smoke. Darren Gill This show is based on a shorter commission for Lucy Guerin’s Pieces in 2024, and it retains the same production team, including lighting designer Rachel Rui Qian Lee and costume designer Geoffrey Watson, who provides beautiful filmy smocks. Tilman Robinson’s score feels a little too insistent. The opening section with its bells has an attractive alienness, but I think the heavier beats used thereafter impose too much on the choreography and a more ambient soundscape might have been more effective.

Advertisement

Editor's pick Updated

Arts Macy Gray concert at Arts Centre cancelled as staff prepare to strike The work is apparently based on the significance of the number seven across religions and cultural traditions. Yet it is strongest when there is no theme: just fleeting relations between bodies – repetitions and doublings, divergences and singularities – in a world before number settles into meaning.

title: You’ve been put on a performance management plan. Are you on the way out?
text:
Advertisement

BusinessWorkplaceWorkplace You’ve been put on a performance management plan. Are you on the way out? Millie Muroi September 13, 2026 — 10:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When roadside patrol mechanic Yep Yap was sacked in 2022, he’d been put on a performance management plan and failed to meet three key performance indicators. But the Fair Work Commission found the targets set for Yap were unrealistic, unachievable and improper, ultimately forcing his employer, the company Club Assist, to reinstate him with back pay under unfair dismissal laws. Performance management plans are increasingly being used as a tick-the-box exercise towards getting rid of people. Stephen Kiprillis Performance management plans, also known as performance improvement plans (PIPs), have become common as a tool towards dismissing an employee. While meant as a genuine way to improve workers’ performance, they are increasingly being used as a tick-the-box exercise towards getting rid of people and still complying with unfair dismissal laws. In fact, these laws – introduced more than 40 years ago to protect workers from arbitrary, unfair sackings – are what have made PIPs so popular in Australia, says Joydeep Hor of employment law firm People + Culture Strategies.

Advertisement

“There’s no hard and fast rule that says you have to have someone on a PIP before you can terminate their employment for performance reasons, but in the absence of one, there can be some questions asked,” Hor says. Related Article Unfair dismissal Minor change to title costs worker her job So, what should you do if you find yourself on a PIP? How do they work? And what do managers need to know? How does a performance management plan work? When publicist Vivian (who did not use her real name because of concern about future employment prospects) was put on a performance management plan at a public relations agency in Sydney this year, it came as a surprise.

Advertisement

She was told not to mention it to colleagues, was given the option to negotiate a settlement instead and was told she had 24 hours to make her decision. The latter, she found out from a lawyer, was not a time frame the firm could hold her to. Vivian had discussions with the firm’s HR department, her employment lawyer and her manager, and agreed on a set of key performance indicators. For the next few months, her performance was closely monitored. Hor says PIPs are intended as a way to hold both employees and managers to account. “The idea is that an employer should be actively working with a so-called ‘underperforming employee’ to help them improve their performance, using a plan which has metrics and timeframes,” he says. However, the process is often treated as more of a set-and-forget process by managers, who Hor says should be setting expectations early and bringing up concerns informally first.

Advertisement

Does it mean you’re about to get sacked? Vivian says getting put on a performance management plan initially felt like she was getting booted. “The process felt micro-manager-y with regular reviews, but the KPIs weren’t hard to turn around, and I ended up passing it,” she says. “It was a bit awkward afterwards, but that didn’t last too long.” TLB Law & Co senior associate Ellie Wolfenden says PIPs have, in some instances, become a tick-the-box exercise rather than a genuine effort to improve employee performance. “It goes towards an employer demonstrating that the employee knew their performance wasn’t meeting the required standard, knew what the required standards were, and had been offered a fair opportunity to improve their performance,” she says.

Advertisement

Wolfenden says that in some situations, employers set benchmarks that are unreasonable or unrealistic. “That’s when employees can feel that the process is not genuinely aimed at improving their performance, but rather is setting them up to fail,” she says. That can be stressful and troubling, but may also create a work health and safety risk the employer needs to manage, she says. What should you do if you’re put on a PIP? Hor says the first step is generally for employees to clarify why it is happening and exactly what is expected. “If there’s anything ambiguous in terms of a target or a deadline, those things should be clarified in a conversation,” he says.

Advertisement

For employees who have been put on a PIP that feels unreasonable, Wolfenden says it can be worth seeking legal advice, clearly documenting why and how any given metrics may be unreasonable, and to weigh in on what they think is achievable. “We’ve seen some performance management plans where sales tasks and targets are wholly out of proportion to the market and an employee is getting held to KPIs that no one in the business is meeting because of external market factors,” she says. Related Article Opinion

Careers The secret skill to getting what you actually want at work Tim Duggan Work columnist In Yap’s case, the employer’s decision to sack him was overruled because the performance metrics – including needing to aim for a particular rate of battery replacements under warranty – were seen as improper, and because many of the firm’s other roadside patrol officers had failed to meet their KPIs without being sacked. Wolfenden says employees on PIPs should document when they are getting positive reviews or feedback from their broader team and external stakeholders, as well as circumstances outside their control that may impact their performance against requirements of the PIP.

Advertisement

Hor says employees who feel they are being managed out should have honest conversations with their managers. “If the employer is just going through the motions, that’s not very nice, and they shouldn’t be, but there may be opportunities to part ways on an agreed basis and short-circuit what could otherwise be a very unpleasant process for all involved,” he says. Negotiating a mutual separation agreement can also be beneficial for the employer in that they can potentially avoid the time and resources involved in managing a PIP process. “PIPs, when done properly, involve weekly check-ins and providing training and support to the employee to help them improve performance,” Wolfenden says. “It’s not meant to be a hands-off process.” What do employers need to know about PIPs? Hor says employers need to ensure the targets they set are clear, measurable and time-bound, with clearly outlined consequences.

Advertisement

Where a metric is subjective, he says the employer should provide details as to how that subjectivity will be assessed. Wolfenden says while there are guidelines available from the Fair Work Ombudsman and theories of best practice from Fair Work Commission decisions and HR professionals, there are no clear regulations around conducting a PIP. Employers need to make sure PIPs are implemented in a reasonable manner, rather than setting workers up to fail. iStock However, employers need to make sure PIPs are implemented in a lawful and reasonable manner, taking into account general work health and safety principles, and the health circumstances of the employee in question, she says: “There is no one-size-fits-all approach.” Wolfenden says it is also important for employers to consider and account for factual matters outside an employee’s control, which may be affecting their performance.

Advertisement

Ultimately, she says performance management plans should be tailored to genuinely help employees improve. Related Article Opinion

Pay My manager wanted me to argue for a pay rise. Why should I? Jonathan Rivett Careers contributor “Using performance management or improvement plans with the aim of exiting the employee from the business, irrespective of performance improvement by the employee, undermines the purpose of such plans and can open the employer up to a claim,” she says. Australian HR Institute chief executive Sarah McCann-Bartlett says employers also need clear documentation and processes around PIPs. “It is now expected that all discussions are documented by the manager as evidence of these conversations and the supports for the employee to improve their performance having been put in place,” she says.

Advertisement

In the case of Yap, for example, the commissioner was concerned there was little documentation explaining the KPIs, or how they were calculated or measured. McCann-Bartlett says there has been a shift recently with the Fair Work Commission requiring that PIPs be carried out reasonably. “The commission has supported terminated employees in their attempts to challenge their termination through unfair dismissal hearings when they have been able to show inconsistencies between the actual process, the employer-employee discussions, what is stated in organisational policies and procedures, and the employee’s job description,” she says. “With more awareness around psychosocial risk, there has been an increase in bullying claims as a result of employees being in a PIP process.” The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. title: Aussies warned as bosses flag 'unusual' reason for upcoming leave rush
text:
The countdown to one of the biggest video game launches in history is already spilling into Aussie workplaces, with one worker claiming so many colleagues have requested time off for Grand Theft Auto VI that HR has flagged the surge as "unusual".

An alleged commercial real estate worker posted online that their team had been warned leave around the game's November 19 release could require "further explanation" because of staff shortages, with the company aware GTA 6 was responsible.

The good news for Aussie workers is bosses can't simply reject annual leave because they think playing GTA 6 is a bad reason to take the day off.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Employment lawyer Michael Byrnes told Yahoo News Australia there was "no obligation" for workers to explain why they wanted to take annual leave, and it was not up to employers to decide whether their plans to binge-play a video game were worthy.

"On the face of it, an employee wanting to take the day off to enjoy the release of GTA 6 is just as legitimate as an employee wanting to go away for a long weekend or attend a wedding," Byrnes said.

"If the employee has accrued annual leave, it is up to them how they use it."

But there is a catch.

Byrnes said employers can refuse leave where approving too many requests for the same day would cause significant operational difficulties or materially compromise customer service.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

And workers who are knocked back should think twice before chucking a launch-day sickie.

"If an employee is falsely claiming to be sick for any reason (including to play GTA 6 upon release) that could be serious misconduct resulting in disciplinary action up to and including summary termination of employment."

An Australian worker claimed their workplace had flagged an "unusual" number of leave requests around the November 19 release of GTA 6.

GTA 6 leave rush could hit Aussie workplaces

The rush for time off could be about to intensify, with recruitment and workplace expert Roxanne Calder telling Yahoo News Australia some businesses could see a "very noticeable concentration" of leave requests, particularly where several serious GTA fans work in the same team.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"If you have five or six serious Grand Theft Auto fans in the same department, November 19 can suddenly become a popular date on the annual-leave calendar," Calder said.

She said the biggest concern for workplaces wasn't teenagers, or even necessarily Gen Z, pointing out the average Australian gamer is now around 35.

"A generation that grew up playing Grand Theft Auto now has jobs, mortgages and leave entitlements. They also have nostalgia," she said.

RELATED:

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Calder said employers should get ahead of the expected demand rather than simply imposing a blanket ban on leave, arguing managers should understand how significant the launch may be to some staff.

Her advice to employers was to embrace the enthusiasm where possible rather than dismiss it.

"Forget the beanbags, listen to your team. Don't judge and accommodate if you can," she said.

Why GTA 6 is such a big deal for Aussies

The hype surrounding Grand Theft Auto VI is difficult to overstate. It is one of the most anticipated entertainment releases in years, arriving after a wait of more than a decade, and following a predecessor that became a global cultural and commercial phenomenon.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

GTA V generated the equivalent of more than $1 billion Australian dollars in just three days when it launched in 2013, becoming the fastest entertainment property in history at the time to reach the billion-dollar milestone. It has since sold more than 200 million copies worldwide, putting enormous expectations on its successor.

Demand for even a glimpse of GTA 6 has been extraordinary. Its first trailer racked up more than 90 million YouTube views in its first 24 hours, setting a record for the biggest non-music video debut on the platform at the time.

Rockstar Games last month took the extraordinary step of premiering a 27-minute extended look at GTA 6 on Netflix, giving subscribers exclusive access for six hours before it was released elsewhere.

The world-first event became a blockbuster itself, attracting 31.1 million views in just four days and becoming Netflix's most-watched title globally for the week, ahead of every movie and television series on the platform.

title: ‘Proud houso’: Albo’s emotional mum defence
text:
Anthony Albanese has declared himself a "proud houso" in response to One Nation leader Pauline Hanson's attack on his late mother.

The Prime Minister's mother, Maryanne Albanese, spent much of her life in public housing in Sydney's Inner West, where she raised her son by herself.

They survived on Ms Albanese's disability pension because severe rheumatoid arthritis crippled her joints.

Mr Albanese often speaks about his mother and poor upbringing, which Senator Hanson dismissed as "pathetic" in an interview this week.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

She said those in public housing on the street where she grew up "had jobs".

"Housing commission houses should not be there for people to live in them for 30, 40 (years), and he said his mother lived in the same one she was born in for 65 years," Senator Hanson told broadcaster-turned-podcaster Karl Stefanovic.

"Sorry, that is not on, to me – it should be limited time.

"You have been given a hand up, move it on to the next ones coming through."

Mr Albanese clapped back on Sunday, giving an emotional defence of his mother and calling her "way out of Pauline Hanson's league".

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese speaks to the media in regard to Pauline Hanson's comments on his mother. Picture: ABC

"Firstly, (Senator Hanson) made comments about me complaining about growing up in public housing – nothing could be further from the truth," he told reporters.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"I'm proud to be a houso and I'm proud of the community in which I grew up.

"I'm also proud about my mother. She was someone who had a tough life. She didn't associate with billionaires."

Mr Albanese's mother met his father while on a cruise in Europe in the early 1960s.

They had a brief romance and she became pregnant.

The relationship did not last because Mr Albanese's father was already committed to another woman in Italy, leaving Ms Albanese to return to Australia and navigate the stigma of having a child out of wedlock.

"She was compassionate, not uncaring. She was generous, not mean. And she was kind, not nasty," Mr Albanese said, pointing to her belief that "there's always someone worse off than yourself".

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"She never complained. She never denigrated anyone. She respected everyone. And I grew up in a community that looked after each other. It was the opposite of being elite."

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese with his mother Maryanne Albanese. Picture: Instagram

He added that he could not understand how Senator Hanson could "attack someone and their character, who died in 2002, some 24 years ago, at age just 65".

"Tell you what's weakness? Nastiness, nastiness and spitefulness and I am stunned at these comments," he said.

"If Pauline Hanson wants to criticise me then that's fine, but my mother was way out of Pauline Hanson's league, way out of it," Mr Albanese said.

﻿'Apologise'

Senator Hanson's comments have sparked condemnation, with Trade Minister Don Farrell earlier on Sunday saying that "attacking somebody's mother … is appalling".

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"It was an appalling remark," he told News24, adding that "Anthony loves his mother".

"I certainly loved my mother. To have them attacked publicly in this way is just appalling.

"There's a certain bitterness in One Nation's approach to the world that I find quite un-Australian".

Trade Minister Don Farrell says One Nation leader Pauline Hanson should apologise. Picture: NewsWire / Brenton Edwards

He called on Senator Hanson to apologise and noted that he "spent almost an hour with Pauline this week going through some of the issues that she's concerned about".

"She wants dignity and respect from her fellow parliamentarians – attacking the Prime Minister's mother like this is not a way to get respect and dignity from your colleagues, and I think Pauline should reflect upon the attack on the Prime Minister's mother and withdraw those comments and apologise," Senator Farrell said.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"I don't think there's any other way forward for her over this issue."

Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie also said that mums were a red line in politics.

Speaking to the same broadcaster, he said the saga was "another indicator to the Australian people" that Senator Hanson was "not fit to be prime minister".

"I reckon mums you leave out of politics," Mr Hastie said.

"I've always tried to be respectful of Pauline."
